teile.einleitung: Submarine cables are cables laid on the sea floor that connect continents with one another. Almost all the internet traffic between the continents flows through them. The first submarine cables were already laid in the 19th century for the telegraph.
wichtigste: About 99 per cent of the data traffic between the continents runs through submarine cables.
The first Atlantic cable of 1858 worked for only about a month.
In 1866 the Great Eastern laid the first transatlantic cable that worked permanently.
TAT-8 was the first fibre-optic cable across the Atlantic in 1988.
Most damage is caused by fishing gear and ships’ anchors.
A deep-sea cable is only about 2.5 centimetres thick.

abschnitte.text: When you open a web page from America on the internet, the data usually travels through a **submarine cable**. About **99 per cent** of the data traffic between the continents runs this way. **Satellites** carry only a small part, because **fibre-optic cables** carry far more data with a shorter delay. In the glass fibres the data travel as **light signals**. On the way, **repeaters** in the cable boost the light again and again.

The first cable across the **Atlantic** was in operation from August **1858**. It carried telegraph messages, but failed after about a month. Too high a voltage had damaged the insulation. In **1866** the steamship **Great Eastern** laid the first transatlantic cable that worked permanently. It was the largest ship in the world at the time and could load the whole cable. Later it also laid cables to India.

**TAT-1** of 1956 was the first telephone cable across the Atlantic. In **1988** came **TAT-8**, the first transatlantic **fibre-optic cable**. It carried data with light instead of with electrical signals in copper. Today many hundreds of submarine cables connect the countries of the world. In the deep sea a modern cable is only about **2.5 centimetres** thick, roughly like a garden hose. Near the coast it is protected with **steel wires** and is thicker.

Most damage occurs unintentionally through the **bottom trawl nets** of fishing and through **ships’ anchors** in shallow coastal waters. There cables are therefore often **buried in the sea floor**. Natural events can destroy cables too. In January 2022 the eruption of the volcano **Hunga Tonga-Hunga Ha’apai** tore apart the only international submarine cable of the island state of **Tonga**. The country was almost cut off from the internet for weeks.

On the coast a submarine cable arrives at a **cable landing station**. There the glass fibres and the power supply for the repeaters end. From there the data continue into the **land network**. A landlocked country such as Switzerland is connected by cables on land to the landing stations in neighbouring countries. Special ships, called **cable ships**, lay and repair the cables.

gewusst: Countries with only one submarine cable are especially vulnerable if it is damaged.
In a repair the cable often has to be brought up to the surface from a depth of thousands of metres.

teile.einleitung: The Río Magdalena is the most important river in Colombia. It flows from the Andes in the south of the country to the Caribbean in the north and for a long time was the country’s most important artery of transport.
wichtigste: The Río Magdalena is the most important river in Colombia.
It rises in the Andes in the south of the country.
It flows north between two mountain ranges of the Andes.
It flows into the Caribbean near the city of Barranquilla.
In the past people and goods travelled on it by riverboat.

abschnitte.titel: From the Andes to the Caribbean
abschnitte.text: The **Río Magdalena** rises in the **Andes** in the south of Colombia. From there it flows for over 1,500 kilometres to the **north**. It flows through a long valley between two mountain ranges of the Andes. Near the city of **Barranquilla** it flows into the **Caribbean**. Many Colombians live in its catchment area.

For a long time there were hardly any good roads through the mountains in Colombia. That is why the Río Magdalena was the most important **artery of transport** in the country. People travelled by **riverboat** from the coast into the interior. Goods such as **coffee** were also carried on the river. Today the river is still important for shipping.

The Río Magdalena also plays a part in literature. The Colombian writer **Gabriel García Márquez** has ships sail on this river in several novels. García Márquez received the **Nobel Prize in Literature** in 1982. For many people in Colombia the river is a part of their history.

gewusst: The river is named after Mary Magdalene, a woman from the Bible.

teile.einleitung: The San Andreas Fault is a huge fracture zone in the Earth’s crust in California. Here two tectonic plates slide past each other. That is why there are repeated strong earthquakes in the area.
wichtigste: The San Andreas Fault is about 1,200 kilometres long.
To the west of it lies the Pacific Plate, to the east the North American Plate.
The plates move right-laterally, which is also called dextral.
In the San Francisco earthquake of 1906 the ground shifted by up to about 6 metres.
Some sections slide slowly and almost without earthquakes, which is called aseismic creep.
At the town of Parkfield the fault is studied especially closely.

abschnitte.titel: Two plates slide past each other
abschnitte.text: The **Pacific Plate** west of the fault moves north-west, the **North American Plate** east of it in the other direction. Such a boundary is called a **transform fault**. If you stand on one side, the other side seems to move to the right. That is why the movement is called **right-lateral** or **dextral**. Each year it amounts to a few centimetres, about as fast as fingernails grow.

The fault is about **1,200 kilometres** long and runs right across California. In the south, near the **Salton Sea**, it passes into the **spreading zone of the Gulf of California**. There parts of the Earth’s crust are moving away from each other. In the north it ends at the **Mendocino Triple Junction** in the sea, where three plates meet.

When the plates catch on each other, tension builds up. When it is suddenly released, the Earth shakes. In 1857 the **Fort Tejon earthquake** shook the south of the fault. In the **San Francisco earthquake** of 1906 the ground shifted by **up to about 6 metres**. After that great fires broke out, and a large part of the city was destroyed.

Not all sections catch. In the middle part the plates slide past each other slowly and almost steadily. This is called **aseismic creep**, because hardly any noticeable earthquakes occur. You can recognise it, for example, in fences, walls and roads that are shifted more and more as time goes on.

At the small town of **Parkfield** moderate earthquakes occurred at strikingly regular intervals. That is why from the 1980s researchers set up many measuring instruments to observe an earthquake closely. The expected earthquake did not come until 2004, much later than thought. In the **SAFOD** project, drilling was done nearby several kilometres deep straight into the active fault.

gewusst: Because the Pacific Plate is moving north-west, Los Angeles and San Francisco come a little closer to each other every year.
In some places you can see how stream beds are shifted sideways at the fault.

teile.einleitung: A seismograph is an instrument that measures and records shaking of the ground. With it experts study earthquakes all over the world. The word comes from Greek and means “shaking writer”.
wichtigste: A seismograph measures ground movements and records them.
Classic instruments use the inertia of a suspended mass.
Modern stations measure in three directions: north-south, east-west and vertical.
In 1889 a distant earthquake from Japan was recorded for the first time in Potsdam.
The record is called a seismogram.
Seismometers can also detect underground nuclear weapons tests.

abschnitte.text: A classic mechanical seismograph is based on **inertia**. A heavy **mass** hangs freely in a housing. When the Earth shakes, the housing moves with the ground, and the mass stays almost at rest because of its inertia. This movement between the mass and the housing is recorded. The sensor is called a **seismometer**. Together with a recorder it makes a **seismograph**, and the result is a **seismogram**.

The ground can move in all **spatial directions**. Modern stations therefore have **three measuring components**: for north-south, east-west and the vertical movement. In this way the whole movement can be reproduced exactly. **Broadband seismometers** measure very fast and very slow vibrations, from fractions of a second to several hundred seconds. Close to the focus of an earthquake **strong-motion accelerometers** are used, so that very strong movements do not overload the instrument.

The British scientist **John Milne** taught in Tokyo in the late 19th century. He built sensitive seismographs with a **horizontal pendulum** and is regarded as one of the fathers of modern seismology. In **1889** **Ernst von Rebeur-Paschwitz** in Potsdam recorded the waves of an earthquake in **Japan**. This showed for the first time that earthquake waves travel through the whole globe. From 1902 **Emil Wiechert** built an earthquake observatory in **Göttingen** with large pendulum seismographs.

In Switzerland too there are earthquakes, mostly small ones. The **Swiss Seismological Service** at ETH Zurich monitors them with a network of measuring stations across the country. The Earth shakes especially often in the **Valais**, in the **Basel** area and in the Grisons. From the measurements experts calculate where an earthquake was and how strong it was. This strength is called the **magnitude**.

Seismometers all over the world supply data for **earthquake research**. From the travel time of the waves people have also learned how the **inside of the Earth** is built. In addition, underground **nuclear explosions** produce ground waves like small earthquakes. The international monitoring system for the **Comprehensive Nuclear-Test-Ban Treaty** therefore uses seismometers to detect such tests.

gewusst: Modern seismometers even sense waves from earthquakes on the other side of the Earth.
The instruments in Göttingen are today a monument to the history of science.

teile.einleitung: The Rhine is one of the largest and most important rivers in Europe. It rises in the Swiss Alps in the canton of the Grisons and flows for about 1,200 kilometres into the North Sea. On the way it forms the famous Rhine Falls and is an important waterway for ships.
wichtigste: The Rhine rises in the canton of the Grisons.
It flows into the North Sea in the Netherlands.
The Rhine flows through Lake Constance, on which Switzerland, Austria and Germany lie.
At Schaffhausen it forms the Rhine Falls, one of the largest waterfalls in Europe.
In Basel lie the Rhine ports, from which cargo ships sail to the North Sea.
The Rhine flows through or along Switzerland, Liechtenstein, Austria, Germany, France and the Netherlands.
It is one of the busiest rivers in the world.

abschnitte.text: The Rhine has two headwaters in the Grisons. The **Vorderrhein** rises at Lake Toma near the Oberalp Pass, the Hinterrhein in the area of the Rheinwaldhorn. At Reichenau near Chur the two flow together. Between Ilanz and Reichenau the Vorderrhein has carved out the **Rhine Gorge**, which is also called the Swiss Grand Canyon.

abschnitte.titel: The way to the North Sea
abschnitte.text: After Chur the Rhine forms the border with Liechtenstein and Austria and then flows into **Lake Constance**. From there it flows west as the High Rhine and largely forms the border between Switzerland and Germany. At Basel it turns north and separates France and Germany. It flows on through Germany to the Netherlands, where it splits up and flows into the North Sea near Rotterdam.

At Neuhausen near **Schaffhausen** the Rhine plunges about 23 metres over a rocky step. The **Rhine Falls** are about 150 metres wide and are regarded as one of the largest waterfalls in Europe. In summer often several hundred cubic metres of water per second tumble down there. You can go by boat as far as a rock in the middle of the waterfall.

The Rhine is one of the most important **waterways** in Europe. From Basel large cargo ships can sail to the North Sea. Through the **Rhine ports** in Basel many goods come into Switzerland, for example heating oil, grain and containers. On the Rhine lie big cities such as Basel, Strasbourg, Cologne, Düsseldorf and Rotterdam, with one of the largest ports in the world.

The Romans already used the Rhine as the border of their empire. On the Middle Rhine in Germany many castles stand on the hills. Well known is the rock **Loreley**, around which grows the legend of a woman who distracted boatmen with her singing. The valley of the Upper Middle Rhine is part of the UNESCO World Heritage.

In 1986 a warehouse of a chemical company burned down at Schweizerhalle near Basel. With the water used to fight the fire, poisons got into the Rhine, and over many kilometres the fish died. After that the **countries along the Rhine** worked together to clean the river, and today the water is much cleaner again. In summer many people in Basel let themselves drift along in a waterproof bag, which is called **Rhine swimming**.

begriffe.erklaerung: The place where a river begins.
The place where a river flows into a sea, a lake or another river.
A river or canal on which ships transport goods.
An area at the mouth where a river splits into many arms.

gewusst: The Rhine is the only river by which Switzerland reaches the sea directly with ships.
The water of the Rhine takes only a few days from Basel to the North Sea.
At the Rhine Falls it was decided in 2021, after years of dispute, not to build a power station.

teile.einleitung: Taiwan is an island in East Asia off the coast of China. It is known for high mountains, large cities and the production of computer chips.
wichtigste: Taiwan lies off the Chinese mainland, separated by the Taiwan Strait.
The capital is Taipei.
In Europe the island used to be called Formosa.
The government in Taipei uses the name Republic of China.
Taiwan is very important worldwide for making computer chips.
The skyscraper Taipei 101 was the tallest building in the world from 2004 to 2010.

abschnitte.text: Taiwan lies in the Pacific off the south-east coast of China. Between the island and the mainland lies the **Taiwan Strait**. Portuguese sailors called the island “**Formosa**”, the beautiful one. Under this name it was long known in Europe. High mountains run through the island, and the highest is almost 4,000 metres high.

After a civil war in China, the government of the **Republic of China** withdrew to Taiwan in 1949. On the mainland the **People's Republic of China** was founded. The government in Taipei still uses the official name **Republic of China** today. The People's Republic regards Taiwan as part of its country, but Taiwan governs itself. Only a few states have official relations with Taiwan, but many, including Switzerland, maintain trade and exchange.

The capital is called **Taipei**. The skyscraper **Taipei 101** stands there, with 101 floors. From **2004 to 2010** it was the **tallest building in the world**. Because Taiwan has earthquakes and typhoons, a giant steel ball hangs inside the tower. It dampens the movements of the building.

Taiwan is especially important worldwide for the production of **computer chips**. These tiny components are found in mobile phones, computers, cars and games consoles. A large share of the world's most advanced chips is made in Taiwan. That is why the whole world is watching the island.

gewusst: The steel ball in Taipei 101 weighs more than 600 tonnes and can be visited.
The Tropic of Cancer runs through Taiwan.

teile.einleitung: The Salar de Uyuni in Bolivia is the largest salt flat in the world. The white, almost perfectly flat surface lies high up on the Altiplano. After rain it turns into a huge mirror.
wichtigste: The Salar de Uyuni is the largest salt flat in the world.
It is over 10,000 square kilometres in size, about a quarter of Switzerland.
It lies at about 3,650 metres in the south-west of Bolivia.
It is the remains of large lakes that dried out long ago.
Under the crust lie large amounts of lithium.
In the rainy season the wet surface reflects the sky.

abschnitte.text: Many thousands of years ago there were large lakes on the **Altiplano**. When they dried up, a thick **salt crust** was left behind. Today the Salar de Uyuni is over 10,000 square kilometres in size. The surface is so level that the difference in height across the whole area is only about one metre. That is why the salt flat is even used to check measuring instruments on **satellites**.

abschnitte.titel: The largest mirror in the world
abschnitte.text: In the **rainy season**, roughly from December to March, a thin layer of water often lies on the salt. Then sky and clouds are reflected so perfectly that you can hardly see the horizon. Many tourists take funny photographs here, because on the white surface it is hard to judge sizes. In the dry season hexagonal patterns form on the crust.

abschnitte.titel: Islands in the middle of the salt
abschnitte.text: In the middle of the salt flat hills rise up that are called **islands**. The best known is **Isla Incahuasi**, on which huge column cacti grow. Around the salt flat there are lagoons in which flamingos live. At the edge there are even hotels whose walls and furniture are built of blocks of salt.

People in the area have long mined **salt** and sold it. Under the crust lies a brine with a great deal of **lithium**, which is needed for batteries. Bolivia would like to make use of this treasure, but the mining is still at the beginning. It also involves the protection of the water and the landscape.

gewusst: The Salar de Uyuni is so bright and large that it can be clearly seen in pictures from space.
At the salt flat there is a graveyard of old steam locomotives that have been rusting there for decades.

teile.einleitung: An emerging economy is a country that is on the way from a developing country to an industrialised country. It stands, so to speak, on the “threshold”. Such countries often grow quickly economically, but still have great differences between rich and poor.
wichtigste: An emerging economy is on the way from a developing country to an industrialised country.
In English such countries are often called “Newly Industrialized Countries”, NIC for short.
Typical are rapid industrialisation and great social differences.
Modern industrial zones and poor rural regions exist side by side.
China is often called the “workshop of the world”.
Well-known groups of emerging economies are BRIC, the Next Eleven and MINT.

abschnitte.text: Emerging economies have rapid **industrialisation**: factories appear, cities grow, and many people move from the country to the city. At the same time there are often still great **social and regional differences**. In English such countries are called **NIC**, which stands for “Newly Industrialized Countries”. The least developed countries, by contrast, are called **LDC**.

In emerging economies there are often two worlds side by side. Experts call this **economic dualism**. Beside highly modern **industrial zones** there are poor rural regions and a large **informal sector**. This includes work without a contract and without insurance, such as street trading. An example of rapid rise is **China**: thanks to export zones and cheap labour it became the **workshop of the world** and the largest exporter of goods.

Countries have tried different strategies. Many Latin American countries from the 1950s relied on **import substitution**. With customs duties they protected an industry of their own, which was meant to replace imported goods. Other countries, for example in East Asia, relied more on **exports**. **Mexico** joined the **OECD** in 1994, an organisation made up mainly of rich industrialised countries. In the same year the free trade agreement **NAFTA** came into force.

For rising countries there are well-known abbreviations. **BRIC** stands for Brazil, Russia, India and China. The economist **Jim O’Neill** named the **Next Eleven** in 2005, eleven further rising countries, including Mexico, Indonesia, Nigeria, Vietnam and South Korea. The group **MINT** stands for Mexico, Indonesia, Nigeria and Turkey. The term was coined by the fund company Fidelity in 2011, and O’Neill made it known from 2013.

Not every emerging economy automatically becomes an industrialised country. When **wages** rise but new ideas and **innovation** are lacking, a country loses its cost advantage. It cannot yet keep up with the high-wage countries, though. Then growth gets stuck. This danger is called the **middle income trap**. Good schools, research and stable institutions are regarded as important for escaping it.

gewusst: Which countries exactly count as emerging economies is not fixed uniformly; different organisations have different lists.
A few decades ago South Korea was a poor country, and today it is one of the great industrial nations.

teile.einleitung: Seals are mammals that live in the sea and are excellent at swimming and diving. They are found mainly in cold seas, from the Arctic to Antarctica.
wichtigste: Seals are mammals and breathe air.
Instead of legs they have flippers.
A thick layer of blubber protects them in ice-cold water.
Seals eat mainly fish.
The elephant seal is the largest seal.
The leopard seal in Antarctica also eats penguins.
The Weddell seal lives furthest south.

abschnitte.text: Seals look a little like fish, but they are **mammals**. They breathe with lungs and have to come to the surface to take in air. Their young drink milk. Instead of legs seals have **flippers**, with which they swim very well. On land, by contrast, they move rather clumsily. Seals include, for example, **harbour seals**, **sea lions** and **walruses**.

Many seals live in ice-cold water. A thick layer of **blubber** under the skin keeps them warm. The blubber also stores energy for times when there is little food. Seals can **dive** for a long time and slow their heartbeat as they do so. In this way they save oxygen. Some species stay under water for more than half an hour.

Seals are **predators**. Most of them eat mainly **fish**, plus squid and crabs. The **leopard seal** in Antarctica is an especially powerful hunter. It also eats **penguins** and sometimes even other seals. With their long whiskers seals sense the movements of fish in the water, even in the dark.

The largest seal is the **elephant seal**. The males have a nose like a small trunk and can weigh several tonnes. The **Weddell seal** lives furthest south, in the ice around Antarctica. It spends the winter under the sea ice. To **take in air**, it keeps **holes in the ice** open with its teeth.

gewusst: There are harbour seals in the North Sea too, for example in the Wadden Sea.
Elephant seals can dive more than a thousand metres deep.

teile.einleitung: Serengeti National Park in Tanzania is one of the most famous national parks in the world. In the wide savannah live lions, elephants, giraffes and huge herds of wildebeest and zebras. The park protects this unique animal paradise.
wichtigste: Serengeti National Park lies in Tanzania.
Life there is determined by the rainy season and the dry season.
The leopard often drags its prey up a tree.
Vultures eat carrion and keep the savannah clean.
The black rhinoceros has become very rare because of poaching.
The giraffe is not one of the “Big Five”.

abschnitte.text: The Serengeti lies close to the **equator**. That is why there is no cold winter there. What matters is whether it is raining or dry. In the **rainy season** fresh grass grows, and the animals find plenty of food. In the **dry season** the grass turns brown, and many animals move to where there is still water and food. That is why large herds of **wildebeest** and **zebras** migrate through the land.

The **“Big Five”** include the **lion**, **leopard**, **elephant**, **rhinoceros** and **Cape buffalo**. The term comes from big-game hunters, for whom these animals were especially difficult to hunt. Today tourists want only to watch and photograph them. The **leopard** is very powerful and climbs well. It often drags its prey up a **tree**, where it is safe from lions and hyenas. The giraffe is **not** one of the Big Five.

The **giraffe** reaches high branches thanks to its long neck. With its tongue, which is up to **50 centimetres** long, it plucks the leaves of the **thorn acacias** from between the thorns. **Hippos** spend the day in the rivers. In this way they protect themselves from the sun. At night they go onto land and eat large amounts of **grass**.

**Vultures** circle over the savannah. They find dead animals from a great height and eat the **carrion**. In this way they help to keep the savannah clean and prevent diseases from spreading. **Hyenas** also eat leftovers that other animals leave behind. In nature every animal has its job.

**Poachers** hunt animals illegally. Rhinoceroses are especially at risk, because their **horn** is sold at a high price in some countries. The **black rhinoceros** has therefore become very rare in the Serengeti and is threatened with extinction. **Rangers** guard the animals and take action against poachers. Income from **tourism** also helps to protect the park.

gewusst: A giraffe needs only a few hours of sleep a day.
Hippos cannot really swim; they walk or bounce along the bottom of the river.

teile.einleitung: Angel Falls in Venezuela is regarded as the highest waterfall in the world. Its water plunges almost a kilometre from a table mountain. It lies in the middle of the rainforest, far from any road.
wichtigste: At about 980 metres, Angel Falls is the highest waterfall in the world.
It plunges from the table mountain Auyán-Tepui in Canaima National Park.
It is named after the American pilot Jimmie Angel.
The Pemón call it Kerepakupai Merú.
Visitors usually reach it by boat and on foot.
In the rainy season the most water flows.

abschnitte.text: Angel Falls is about **980 metres** high in all, and the water drops over 800 metres in free fall. This makes it about **three times as high** as the Staubbach Falls in Lauterbrunnen. On the long way down a large part of the water is turned to spray by the wind. It arrives below as a fine **mist**. In the **rainy season** the fall is mighty, in the dry season sometimes only a thin veil.

abschnitte.titel: A table mountain in the rainforest
abschnitte.text: The water falls from **Auyán-Tepui**, a **table mountain**. This is what mountains with steep rock walls and a flat top that looks like a table are called. In the language of the Pemón they are called tepui. The waterfall lies in **Canaima National Park**, which is part of the UNESCO World Heritage. The rocks of the table mountains are among the oldest rocks on Earth.

The waterfall is named after the American pilot **Jimmie Angel**. He flew over the area in the 1930s and made the fall known. In 1937 he landed on the table mountain, but his aeroplane got stuck in a **bog**. Angel and his companions had to climb down into the valley on foot, which took days. The local **Pemón** call the fall **Kerepakupai Merú**.

No road leads to Angel Falls. Most visitors first fly in a small aeroplane to the village of **Canaima**. From there they travel several hours upriver in a wooden boat. After that they go on foot through the rainforest to a viewpoint. Because the rivers carry little water in the dry season, boat trips are possible mainly in the rainy season.

gewusst: Jimmie Angel’s aeroplane stayed on the table mountain for over 30 years before it was recovered. Today it stands in front of the airport of the city of Ciudad Bolívar.
The top of the waterfall is often hidden in cloud, so that you cannot see all of it.

teile.einleitung: Switzerland has no sea, yet ocean-going ships sail the oceans under the Swiss flag. These ships make up the Swiss ocean-going fleet. It was founded in the Second World War to supply the country with important goods.
wichtigste: The Swiss ocean-going fleet was founded in 1941.
In the Second World War it was meant to secure the supply of Switzerland.
With its own ships Switzerland could import food and raw materials.
The home port of the ships is Basel.
The fleet belongs to shipping companies, not to the state.

abschnitte.text: In the **Second World War** Switzerland was surrounded by countries at war. Many foreign ships were no longer available to transport goods for Switzerland. That is why the country had to rely on **its own ships** to import **food** and **raw materials**. Since **1941**, therefore, ocean-going ships have sailed under the Swiss flag. As ships of a neutral country they could bring goods across the sea in this difficult time.

Every ship is registered in a **home port**. For the Swiss ocean-going ships this is **Basel**, although the large ships can never dock there. Basel is connected to the North Sea by the **Rhine** and is the Swiss place for shipping. The ships belong to private **shipping companies**, that is, firms that operate ships. In an emergency the Confederation can fall back on them so that the **national supply** is secured.

abschnitte.titel: A landlocked country on the sea
abschnitte.text: That a country without a sea coast has an ocean-going fleet is unusual, but permitted. Landlocked states, too, may let ships sail the seas under their flag. The number of Swiss ocean-going ships has changed greatly over time. In the 2010s some shipping companies ran into **financial difficulties**, and the Confederation had to pay on guarantees. This was much discussed in politics.

gewusst: On Swiss ocean-going ships the red flag with the white cross flies, though in a rectangular form.
Basel is the home port of ships that can never sail as far as Basel.

teile.einleitung: The journey to school is the way from home to school. Children all over the world make it in very different ways: on foot, by bicycle, by bus or even by boat. On the way, road safety is especially important.
wichtigste: Many children in Switzerland walk to school.
Before a road the Swiss saying applies: “Warte, luege, lose, laufe” (wait, look, listen, go).
The safest way to cross the road is at the zebra crossing.
Reflective strips help you to be seen in the dark.
In the USA many children go by yellow school buses.
In Bangladesh some children go to school by boat.

abschnitte.text: Many children in Switzerland go to school **on foot**. On the way they often meet other children, chat and get exercise in the fresh air. In this way they also learn to find their own way in **traffic**. In some communities children who live far away go by **school bus** or PostBus.

In Switzerland children learn the saying **“Warte, luege, lose, laufe”**, which is Swiss German for wait, look, listen, go. You wait at the side of the road, look, listen and only then cross. The **zebra crossing** is the safest, because cars have to stop there. Even so, you look first left, then right and left again. In the dark, light-coloured clothes and **reflective strips** help: they shine when car lights fall on them, and so drivers see the children early.

In the **USA** many children go to school by school bus. These buses are **yellow**, so that they can be seen well in traffic. In the **Netherlands** the land is flat and there are very many **cycle paths**. That is why especially many children go to school by **bicycle** there, often from a young age.

In **Bangladesh** there are often **floods**. When everything is under water, some children come to school by **boat**. There are even schools on boats there, which pick the children up and teach them on the water. In some countries there are only a few schools in the countryside and no bus. There children sometimes walk **for more than an hour** to school.

In many countries children wear the same clothes at school, a **school uniform**. This is usual, for example, in **England**, but also in Japan or in many countries of Africa. Often it includes a shirt or blouse, a jumper in the school’s colour and sometimes a tie. In Switzerland public schools mostly have **no** uniform.

gewusst: The saying “Warte, luege, lose, laufe” is Swiss German and means “wait, look, listen, go”.
The yellow colour of American school buses even has a name of its own: “School Bus Yellow”.

teile.einleitung: Black earth is one of the most fertile soils in the world. It has a very thick, dark layer of humus and forms mainly in steppes. Under its Russian name it is called chernozem.
wichtigste: Black earth is called chernozem in Russian, which means “black earth”.
It forms in the steppe, mostly on loess.
Its dark humus layer can become more than a metre thick.
Burrowing animals such as ground squirrels and hamsters mix the soil.
Ukraine is known for its large areas of black earth.
There is also black earth in the Magdeburg Börde in Germany.

abschnitte.text: Black earth is a **type of soil** with a very thick, dark top layer. Soil scientists call this layer the **A horizon**, and it is rich in **humus**, that is, in decomposed plant remains. It can become **more than a metre** thick. The Russian name **chernozem** means “black earth”. The Russian soil scientist **Vasily Dokuchaev** described this soil in detail at the end of the 19th century.

Black earth forms in the **steppe**, a wide grassland. The dense **root system** of the steppe grasses supplies a lot of plant material. In the **cold winter** and the **dry summer** it is broken down only slowly. In this way more humus stays in the soil than is lost. Over thousands of years a very thick layer of humus forms. Black earth is also found under the **tallgrass prairie** in North America.

Black earth usually develops on **loess**. Loess is a fine, **chalky** material that the wind deposited in the Ice Age. It is loose and rich in minerals and therefore ideal for a fertile soil. Under the dark humus layer there often follows directly the pale, chalky loess.

In black earth live many burrowing animals such as **ground squirrels**, **hamsters** and earthworms. They turn the soil over and carry humus down into the depths. Their old burrows fill up with soil material. These filled burrows are called **krotovinas**. In the soil profile you recognise them as dark or pale patches.

A large part of **Ukraine** is covered with black earth. That is why the country is often called the “breadbasket of Europe”. It is one of the important exporters of **wheat**, **maize** and sunflower oil. In Germany the **Magdeburg Börde** has especially good black earth soils. In the German soil rating they reach up to **100 points**, the highest value. There mainly wheat and **sugar beet** are grown.

gewusst: A layer of humus over a metre thick needs thousands of years to form.
The soil rating in Germany measures the fertility of a soil in points up to 100.

teile.einleitung: In open-cast mining, raw materials are taken straight from the Earth's surface in huge, open pits. This is how brown coal is mined, for example, but also copper, gravel or rock.
wichtigste: Open-cast mining means extraction in open pits at the surface.
The opposite is underground mining in tunnels and shafts.
Brown coal is often mined in open-cast mines.
Giant excavators first remove the layers of earth on top.
After mining, the pits are often turned into lakes or forests.

abschnitte.text: In **open-cast mining** people do not work in tunnels underground but in **open pits**. This is worthwhile when a raw material does not lie very deep. **Brown coal** often lies only a few dozen to a few hundred metres below the surface. That is why it is usually mined in open-cast mines. The opposite is called **underground mining**, as in a mine with shafts.

Above the raw material lie soil, sand and rock. These layers are called **overburden**. Huge **bucket-wheel excavators** remove it and then dig out the coal. These excavators are among the largest moving machines in the world. Conveyor belts carry the coal to power stations, where it is used to produce electricity.

abschnitte.titel: Effects on the landscape and on people
abschnitte.text: An open-cast mine needs a great deal of space. In Germany, whole villages had to make way for brown coal mines, and the people moved to new places. To keep the pit dry, **groundwater** is pumped away. In addition, burning coal produces a lot of **CO₂**, which warms the Earth. That is why coal mining is highly controversial.

When mining is finished, the landscape is **restored**, which means it is put back in order. Forests are planted, fields are laid out, or the pit is allowed to fill with water. In the **Lusatian Lake District** in Germany, for example, many new lakes have appeared this way. In Switzerland there are no open-cast coal mines, but there are many **gravel pits** and **quarries**, which also work at the surface.

gewusst: A bucket-wheel excavator can be as big as a skyscraper lying on its side.
Copper and gold are also often extracted in huge open-cast mines.

teile.einleitung: In a grid plan the streets of a town are laid out like a lattice. They cross at right angles, and between them lie rectangular blocks of buildings. This way of building is already over 2,000 years old.
wichtigste: In a grid plan the streets cross at right angles.
The Greek Hippodamus of Miletus is regarded as the originator of this kind of planning.
Roman camps had two main streets: the Cardo and the Decumanus.
Mannheim is called the City of Squares because of its grid.
La Chaux-de-Fonds is a UNESCO World Heritage site for its rectangular layout.
The plan of 1811 fixed the street grid of Manhattan.

abschnitte.text: Already in antiquity towns were planned as a grid. The Greek town planner **Hippodamus of Miletus** lived in the 5th century BC. After him people speak of the **Hippodamian plan**. The Romans too built their military camps and many towns at right angles. The two main streets were called the **Cardo** and the **Decumanus**, and they crossed in the middle.

The German city of **Mannheim** is called the **City of Squares** because of its grid: the blocks of the city centre carry letters and numbers instead of street names, for example C 4. In Switzerland **La Chaux-de-Fonds** is well known. After a great fire in 1794 the watchmaking town was rebuilt with parallel streets. Since 2009 La Chaux-de-Fonds and Le Locle have been part of the **UNESCO World Heritage**.

In 1682 **William Penn** planned the city of **Philadelphia** with a grid and five squares. In 1785 the **Land Ordinance** divided the land west of the first states into squares. A **township** is a square of six miles by six miles and contains **36 sections**. The advantage: the land could easily be **surveyed and sold**. That is why in the Midwest you still see perfectly straight roads and square fields today.

The **Commissioners’ Plan** of 1811 fixed the street grid of **Manhattan** in New York. The avenues run lengthways, the numbered streets across them. The grid is slightly rotated and follows the shape of the island. Twice a year, at the end of May and in July, the sun sets exactly along the axis of the cross streets. This spectacle is called **Manhattanhenge**.

gewusst: The name Manhattanhenge alludes to Stonehenge in England, where on certain days the sun likewise rises exactly between the stones.
In Mannheim an address is, for example, simply Q 5 with a house number.

teile.einleitung: Neuschwanstein Castle is one of the best-known castles in the world. It stands in Bavaria in Germany, high on a rock near the town of Füssen. It looks like a fairy-tale castle, but was built only in the 19th century.
wichtigste: Neuschwanstein stands in Bavaria, near the town of Füssen.
King Ludwig II of Bavaria had it built.
Building began in 1869.
The name contains the swan, the king’s favourite animal.
Since 1886 visitors have been allowed inside.
Well over a million people come every year.

abschnitte.text: The castle was built for King **Ludwig II** of Bavaria. He spent part of his childhood in the yellow castle of **Hohenschwangau**, which lies opposite. From there he saw the rock on which he later had his own castle built. Ludwig II loved music, especially the operas of **Richard Wagner**, and old legends. Because of his splendid castles he is often called the “Fairy-Tale King”.

The name **Neuschwanstein** contains the word for **swan**. The king loved swans, because they appear in old legends and in Wagner’s opera about the Swan Knight. In the castle you find many swans in pictures, on door handles and in decorations. The walls of many rooms are decorated with large **paintings** of legends.

The foundation stone was laid in **1869**. The castle looks like a castle from the **Middle Ages**, but it is much younger. For the time it had modern **technology**: heating, running water and **flush toilets**. The castle was never quite finished, and many planned rooms stayed empty. The king lived in it only for a short time.

abschnitte.titel: Visitors from all over the world
abschnitte.text: Ludwig II died in **1886**. Only a few weeks after his death the castle was opened to **visitors**. Today well **over a million** people from all over the world come every year. Many travel in through the nearby town of **Füssen**. Neuschwanstein is among the most popular sights in Europe.

The castle is so famous that it has influenced other buildings. **Walt Disney** drew inspiration from Neuschwanstein. His **Sleeping Beauty Castle** at Disneyland looks similar to it. In this way many children know the castle without ever having been to Bavaria.

gewusst: From the Marienbrücke bridge over a deep gorge you have one of the most beautiful views of the castle.
The castle was built when there were already railways and photography.

teile.einleitung: Robert Falcon Scott was a British naval officer and polar explorer. In January 1912 he reached the South Pole, but the Norwegian Roald Amundsen had already been there before him.
wichtigste: Robert Falcon Scott came from Great Britain.
His South Pole expedition of 1910 to 1913 is named after the ship Terra Nova.
As draught animals he used mainly ponies, besides dogs.
In January 1912 his party reached the South Pole.
There they found a tent with a Norwegian flag.
On the way back all five men died.
From his diaries, which were found, we know what happened.

abschnitte.text: Robert Falcon Scott was born in 1868 in **Great Britain** and was an officer in the navy. Already from 1901 to 1904 he led an expedition to **Antarctica**. After that he wanted to be the first to reach the **South Pole**. For this he set off in 1910 with the ship **Terra Nova**. The whole expedition is named after this ship.

Scott used mainly **ponies** as draught animals, plus dogs and some **motor sledges**. The motor sledges soon broke down in the cold. The ponies did not cope well with ice and snow. That is why the men had to pull their heavy sledges themselves on the last part of the way. This took an enormous amount of strength.

In **January 1912** Scott and four companions reached the South Pole. There they found a **tent with a Norwegian flag**. Roald Amundsen had arrived a good month before them. For Scott and his men this was a great disappointment. Now the long way back through ice and storm lay ahead of them.

On the way back it grew colder and colder, and the supplies were not enough. **All five men died**. The sick **Lawrence Oates** left the tent one day with the words that he was just going outside for a moment. He did not want to hold the others back. Only months later did a search party find the tent with Scott and two companions. From Scott’s **diaries** we know exactly today what happened on the journey.

gewusst: The research station at the South Pole is called the Amundsen-Scott South Pole Station.
On the way back Scott’s party carried many rock samples, which were important for research.

teile.einleitung: Tasmania is a large island south of Australia. It is the smallest state of Australia and is known for its wild nature and the Tasmanian devil.
wichtigste: Tasmania lies south of the Australian mainland.
The Bass Strait separates the island from the mainland.
Tasmania is the smallest state of Australia, and its capital is Hobart.
The island is named after the navigator Abel Tasman.
The Tasmanian devil now lives in the wild almost only here.
The thylacine used to live in Tasmania and is extinct.

abschnitte.text: Tasmania lies **south of Australia**. The **Bass Strait** separates the island from the mainland. Tasmania is the **smallest state** of Australia. The capital is called **Hobart**. The climate is **cooler** and damper than in the north of Australia, and in winter snow even falls in the mountains.

The Dutch navigator **Abel Tasman** reached the island in 1642 as the first European. At first he called it Van Diemen's Land. Later it was named **Tasmania** in his honour. Long before the Europeans came, Aboriginal people, the original inhabitants, already lived here.

abschnitte.titel: The Tasmanian devil and the thylacine
abschnitte.text: The **Tasmanian devil** is a small, black predator with a loud screech. In the wild it now lives almost only in Tasmania. A contagious disease has killed many Tasmanian devils, which is why it is protected. The **thylacine**, with its striped back, also used to live in Tasmania. Today it is **extinct**, and the last known animal died in a zoo in 1936.

A large part of Tasmania is wilderness with rainforest, mountains and lakes. **Cradle Mountain** is well known, with many hiking trails. The wilderness of Tasmania is a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Wombats and platypuses also live there.

In the past Britain sent convicted people to Australia. At **Port Arthur** there was a large **convict colony**, which means a prison camp. The old stone buildings are still standing and are now a museum. Today they are part of a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

gewusst: For its size, the Tasmanian devil can bite very hard.
Hobart was founded in 1804 and, after Sydney, is the oldest capital of an Australian state.

teile.einleitung: Tanzania is a country in East Africa on the Indian Ocean. It is famous for Kilimanjaro, the Serengeti and the island of Zanzibar.
wichtigste: The capital of Tanzania is Dodoma, and the largest city is Dar es Salaam.
Kilimanjaro is the highest mountain in Africa.
The island of Zanzibar lies off the coast.
The money is called the Tanzanian shilling.
Chimpanzees live in Gombe National Park.
Lake Tanganyika lies in the west.

abschnitte.titel: A country on the Indian Ocean
abschnitte.text: Tanzania lies in **East Africa** on the **Indian Ocean**. The capital is **Dodoma**, inland. The largest city is **Dar es Salaam** on the coast, with an important port. The country was formed in 1964 from the mainland of **Tanganyika** and the island of **Zanzibar**. The most important language is **Kiswahili**, and the money is called the **Tanzanian shilling**.

In the north stands **Kilimanjaro**, the highest mountain in Africa, almost 5,900 metres high. Its summit carries ice even though it is close to the equator. On the **western border** lies the long and very deep **Lake Tanganyika**, and in the north Lake Victoria. In the south-west lies Lake Malawi.

Tanzania has many famous national parks. In the **Serengeti**, huge herds of wildebeest and zebras roam every year. In the **Ngorongoro Crater**, many wild animals live close together, including lions and rhinos. **Tarangire** park is known for its many elephants and thick **baobab trees**. In **Gombe National Park** on Lake Tanganyika you can watch **chimpanzees**.

The island of **Zanzibar** lies off the coast. It used to be an important trading place for **spices** such as cloves. The old town, “Stone Town”, is a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Today many tourists come for the white beaches and the warm sea.

gewusst: The Ngorongoro Crater is a huge collapsed volcano.
The researcher Jane Goodall began observing chimpanzees in Gombe in 1960.

teile.einleitung: Starfish are star-shaped sea animals that crawl slowly over the sea floor. Most have five arms. They are not fish, but belong to the echinoderms.
wichtigste: Most starfish have five arms.
Starfish belong to the echinoderms.
They live only in the salty sea.
They crawl with many small tube feet.
At the tips of their arms they have simple eyes.
Their mouth lies underneath, in the middle.

abschnitte.titel: A star made of five parts
abschnitte.text: Most starfish have **five arms**. There are also species with many more arms, though. Their body is divided into five equal parts, which is called **five-fold symmetry**. Starfish belong to the **echinoderms**, because their skin often has small **spines**. A close relative is the **sea urchin**, which is also built with five-fold symmetry. Starfish come in many colours, from orange and red to blue.

On the underside of its arms the starfish has many tiny **tube feet**. They are filled with water and can suck themselves fast. With them the starfish **crawls** slowly over stones and sand. At the tip of each **arm** sits a simple **eye**. With it the starfish tells light from dark, but sees no exact pictures.

The starfish’s **mouth** lies on the **underside**, exactly in the middle. Many starfish eat **mussels**. With its tube feet the starfish pulls the shells of a mussel open a crack. Then it **pushes its stomach** out into the mussel and digests it there. The prey is therefore digested outside the body.

Starfish need **salt water**. That is why they live only in the **sea** and never in lakes or rivers. They are found in all oceans, from the shallow beach to the **deep sea**. Some starfish can **regrow** a lost arm. This helps them when an enemy has attacked them.

gewusst: Starfish have no brain, only a ring of nerves around the mouth.
In some species a torn-off arm can grow back.

teile.einleitung: The horse latitudes are areas of weak wind on both sides of the equator, at about 30 degrees of latitude. Sailing ships used to fear them, because there for days on end hardly any wind blew.
wichtigste: The horse latitudes lie at about 30 degrees north and south latitude.
There lie the subtropical high pressure belts.
Weak winds and little precipitation are typical.
From the horse latitudes the trade winds blow towards the equator and the westerlies towards the poles.
The Azores High belongs to the high pressure belt of the northern hemisphere.
The Sargasso Sea in the North Atlantic lies in the horse latitudes.
Because a lot of water evaporates and little rain falls, the sea there is especially salty.

abschnitte.text: The name **horse latitudes** is very old. A widespread explanation goes like this: sailing ships there often got into a **calm**, that is, a lack of wind. The voyage then took much longer, and drinking water and fodder ran short. That is why **horses** are said to have been thrown overboard. Whether that was really so is not quite certain. In English the areas are called “horse latitudes”.

At the equator warm air rises. At great height it flows towards the poles and sinks again at about **30 degrees of latitude**. There the **subtropical high pressure belts** form. The **sinking air** warms up, and as a result clouds dissolve. That is why it rarely rains in the horse latitudes. In this belt lie large deserts such as the **Sahara**.

In the horse latitudes themselves it is often calm. At ground level, however, the air flows out of the high pressure area. Towards the equator blow the **trade winds**, steady winds that seafarers once liked to use. Towards the poles blow the **westerlies**. These westerlies often bring Switzerland weather from the Atlantic too.

The **Azores High** over the Atlantic belongs to the high pressure belt of the northern hemisphere. It is very important for the weather in Europe. In summer the high pressure belt **shifts** to the north. That is why summers on the **Mediterranean** are mostly hot and dry. When the Azores High reaches far to the north, it brings Switzerland fine summer weather too.

In the horse latitudes of the North Atlantic lies the **Sargasso Sea**. It is known for its calm and for **drifting seaweed** that floats on the surface of the water. Because in the horse latitudes a lot of water **evaporates** and little rain falls, the **salt content** of the sea there is especially high.

gewusst: The Sargasso Sea is a sea with no coast at all; it is bounded only by ocean currents.
Many of the largest deserts on Earth lie near the horse latitudes.

teile.einleitung: The Sahel is a broad belt in Africa that stretches south of the Sahara from the Atlantic to the Red Sea. Here the desert gradually turns into savannah. People’s lives depend strongly on the scarce rain.
wichtigste: The Sahel lies between the Sahara in the north and the damper savannah in the south.
Only about 100 to 600 millimetres of rain fall a year, mostly in a few summer months.
Typical plants are grasses, thorn bushes, acacias and baobabs.
In the 1970s and 1980s there were severe droughts and famines.
The Sahel states include Senegal, Mauritania, Mali, Burkina Faso, Niger and Chad.
The Great Green Wall is meant to slow the spread of the desert.

abschnitte.text: The name **Sahel** comes from Arabic and probably means **shore** or **coast**. For caravans that had crossed the Sahara, the Sahel was like the saving shore of a sea of sand. The belt reaches from Senegal and Mauritania in the west to Sudan and Eritrea in the east. It is a few hundred kilometres wide and several thousand kilometres long.

abschnitte.titel: Little rain, a lot of dust
abschnitte.text: In the north of the Sahel only about 100 millimetres of rain fall a year, in the south about 600 millimetres. By comparison: in Zurich it is over 1,000 millimetres. The rain comes almost only in the **rainy season** in summer, and the rest of the year is dry. In winter the **Harmattan** often blows, a dry north-east wind from the Sahara. It brings dust and cool nights as far as the Gulf of Guinea.

Many families grow **millet**, a grain that needs little water and grows on barren soils. Many herders live as **nomads**: they follow the rain and the fresh grass with cattle, goats, sheep and camels. In this way they make the best use of the scarce pastures. Trees such as acacias and the thick **baobab** provide shade, fodder and fruit.

In the 1970s and 1980s the rain stayed away for several years. Harvests failed, many animals died, and many people went hungry or had to leave their homes. When drought, **overgrazing** and deforestation come together, the soil loses its plant cover. It dries out, and areas like deserts form. This process is called **desertification**.

In 2007 the African Union launched the **Great Green Wall** project. Right across the Sahel, from Senegal to Djibouti, a belt of trees, shrubs and greened areas is to be created. It is meant to protect the soil and help people to grow more again. The project is making good progress in some countries, in others only slowly.

gewusst: Saharan dust that the wind carries across the Sahel can fly as far as Europe and sometimes even colours the snow in the Swiss Alps yellowish.
The baobab can store a lot of water in its thick trunk and so survive long dry spells.

teile.einleitung: A savannah is a wide grassland with scattered trees. It usually lies between the rainforest and the desert. The savannahs of Africa, with lions, elephants and giraffes, are especially well known.
wichtigste: In the savannah mainly grass grows, with scattered trees.
It usually lies between rainforest and desert.
There is a rainy season and a dry season.
Large savannahs with lions are found in Africa.
Typical animals are the giraffe, zebra, elephant and cheetah.
The Serengeti in Tanzania is a famous national park.

abschnitte.titel: Grass as far as the eye can see
abschnitte.text: The **savannah** is a landscape with a lot of **grass** and only scattered trees or shrubs. The grass can grow taller than a child. Savannahs usually lie **between the rainforest and the desert**. The largest are in **Africa**, but savannahs are also found in South America, India and Australia.

The climate of the savannah has two main seasons. In the **rainy season** a lot of rain falls, the grass turns green and the animals find enough food. In the **dry season** it hardly rains for months, the grass turns yellow and many waterholes dry up. Then many animals travel long distances in search of water and grass.

A typical tree of the African savannah is the **baobab**. Its trunk is very thick and can store a lot of water. In the dry season it loses its leaves to save water. **Acacias** with flat, umbrella-shaped crowns also grow in the savannah.

The **giraffe** uses its long neck to eat leaves high up in the trees. **Zebras** are recognised by their black and white stripes. The **African elephant** is the largest land animal in the world. The **cheetah** is the fastest land animal and can briefly reach over 90 kilometres an hour. Lions, rhinoceroses, antelopes and wildebeest also live here.

A famous national park with savannah is the **Serengeti** in **Tanzania**. Every year over a million **wildebeest**, together with zebras and gazelles, travel in a great circle through the land. They follow the rain and the fresh grass. The Serengeti is part of the UNESCO World Heritage.

gewusst: A cheetah can run very fast, but can keep up the speed only for a short time.
Some baobabs are over a thousand years old.

teile.einleitung: Lake Tanganyika is a huge lake in East Africa. It is the longest freshwater lake on Earth and is famous for its many colourful fish.
wichtigste: Lake Tanganyika is the longest freshwater lake on Earth, about 670 kilometres.
It borders four countries: Tanzania, Congo, Burundi and Zambia.
It lies in the East African Rift Valley.
About 250 species of cichlids live in the lake.
Water flows out towards the Congo via the River Lukuga.

abschnitte.text: Lake Tanganyika is about **670 kilometres long**, but mostly only about 50 kilometres wide. No other freshwater lake is as long. It is also very deep, the **second deepest lake** on Earth after Lake Baikal. **Four countries** lie on its shore: **Tanzania**, the **Democratic Republic of the Congo**, **Burundi** and **Zambia**. Tanzania and Congo have the largest shares.

The lake lies in the **East African Rift Valley**. There the **Earth's crust** is slowly drifting apart, and the ground sinks between steep edges. Water collected in this rift. The lake is several million years old. Water flows out to the west via the **River Lukuga** and reaches the **Congo** and finally the Atlantic.

About **250 species** of **cichlids** live in Lake Tanganyika. Most of them are found nowhere else in the world. In the very old lake they developed over a long time into many species. That is why the lake is famous among **researchers** and aquarium lovers. For the people on the shore, fishing is very important.

In 1858 the British explorers **Richard Burton** and **John Speke** were the first Europeans to reach the lake. They were looking for the sources of the Nile. In 1871 **Henry Morton Stanley** found the missing explorer **David Livingstone** in **Ujiji** on the lakeshore. He is said to have greeted him with the famous words “Dr Livingstone, I presume?”

gewusst: On the shore of the lake lies Gombe National Park, where Jane Goodall studied chimpanzees.
After Lake Baikal, Lake Tanganyika holds the most fresh water of any lake.

teile.einleitung: The sector model is a model that describes how cities are laid out. It shows the city like a cake with slices that reach outwards from the centre. The economist Homer Hoyt presented it in 1939.
wichtigste: Homer Hoyt developed the sector model in 1939.
The zones have the shape of slices of cake.
The sectors are arranged mainly along transport routes.
For this Hoyt analysed rents of homes.
All the sectors start from the business centre.
Critics complain that the model knows only one centre.

abschnitte.text: In the sector model the **business centre** lies in the middle. From there the areas radiate **wedge-shaped** outwards, like the slices of a **cake**. Each of these **sectors** has its own use, such as industry, workers’ districts or residential areas of the upper class. The sectors are arranged mainly along **transport routes**, that is, along roads, railway lines or rivers.

The economist **Homer Hoyt** published the model in **1939** in a study for the Federal Housing Administration, the US federal agency for housing loans. He studied many cities in the USA and mapped the average **rents** per block of buildings. It showed that areas with high rents had the shape of **sectors** and not of rings.

Wealthy households prefer axes with good **transport links**, a nice view or a position away from industry, often on **high ground**. The **workers’ housing area**, by contrast, lies next to the **industrial sector**, close to the factories and railway lines. In this way journeys to work are short. The upper class avoids this direction because of noise and exhaust fumes. When the city grows, a better residential area continues outwards in the **same sector**.

Hoyt built on an older model, the **concentric zone model**. In it the land uses lie in rings around the centre. The sector model extends this idea with **wedges** along the transport routes. Like the concentric zone model, however, the sector model also starts from only **one centre**. Modern cities, though, often have **several centres**. That is why other researchers later developed the **multiple nuclei model**.

A model of a city is a **simplification**. No real city looks exactly like the model. Even so, such models help to recognise patterns, for example why districts along a railway line develop in a similar way. In **geography lessons** a real city is often compared with different models, including cities in Switzerland.

gewusst: Hoyt’s model is based on data from over 140 cities in the USA.
In many cities industrial areas still lie along railway lines and rivers today.

teile.einleitung: Many countries own valuable natural resources such as oil, gas or diamonds. Surprisingly, some of these countries still do badly economically. This puzzle is called the resource curse.
wichtigste: The British economist Richard Auty coined the term “resource curse” in 1993.
In English it is also called the “Paradox of Plenty”.
“Dutch disease” weakens other industries through a strong currency.
A rentier state is financed mainly from income from raw materials instead of from taxes.
Because raw material prices fluctuate greatly, state income fluctuates too.
Norway invests its oil income abroad in a sovereign wealth fund.
The EITI initiative campaigns for transparency in the raw materials sector.

abschnitte.titel: Rich in raw materials, poor in growth
abschnitte.text: A **resource curse** exists when a country grows more slowly than other countries despite rich natural resources. The term was coined by the British economist **Richard Auty** in 1993. In English it is called the **resource curse** or also the **Paradox of Plenty**. There are various reasons for it. Not every country rich in raw materials is affected, however.

When a country sells many raw materials, a lot of foreign money flows into the country. This makes its own **currency** more valuable. Other goods from this country become more expensive abroad and sell less well. As a result **industry** and other export sectors suffer. This effect is called **Dutch disease**, because it was observed in the Netherlands after large finds of natural gas.

A state that is financed mainly from income from raw materials instead of from taxes is called a **rentier state**. Experts suspect that the government then depends less on its citizens. A further problem: **raw material prices fluctuate greatly**. If the price falls, the state suddenly lacks a lot of money. **Venezuela** has the largest oil reserves in the world and fell into a severe economic crisis after the collapse in the oil price from 2014.

**Norway** is seen as an example of how to avoid the resource curse. The country invests its oil income abroad in a large **sovereign wealth fund**. In this way the economy is not flooded with money, and the wealth is kept for later generations. **Saudi Arabia** wants to make its economy less dependent on oil with the plan **Vision 2030**. The **EITI** initiative demands transparency about payments in the raw materials sector, so that it becomes visible where the money goes.

Switzerland itself has hardly any natural resources. Even so, it is very important in the raw materials business. Many large **commodity trading firms** have their headquarters in Switzerland. **Geneva** is regarded as one of the most important trading centres for oil in the world. Switzerland also supports the **EITI** initiative.

gewusst: Botswana is seen as an example showing that income from diamonds can also lead to prosperity.
The Norwegian sovereign wealth fund is one of the largest sovereign wealth funds in the world.

teile.einleitung: Samarkand is one of the oldest cities in Central Asia and lies in Uzbekistan. It was an important stop on the Silk Road. Its blue domes and magnificent buildings are famous all over the world.
wichtigste: Samarkand lies in Uzbekistan and is over 2,000 years old.
In the Middle Ages the city became rich through trade on the Silk Road.
In the 14th century Timur made Samarkand the capital of his empire.
The Registan is a square surrounded by three madrasas.
Timur’s grandson Ulugh Beg had a famous observatory built.
Blue tiles and domes shape the buildings of the city.

abschnitte.titel: A city on the Silk Road
abschnitte.text: Samarkand is one of the oldest cities in Central Asia. Even Alexander the Great came here; at that time the city was called **Maracanda**. Because it lay on the **Silk Road**, many caravans with silk, spices, paper and other goods passed through the city. Merchants from China, Persia and India met here. In this way Samarkand became very rich in the Middle Ages.

In the 14th century the ruler **Timur** made Samarkand the capital of his great empire. He conquered wide areas in Asia and brought craftsmen and artists from many countries to his city. They built magnificent mosques, palaces and tombs. Timur himself lies buried in the **Gur-e-Amir** mausoleum.

The **Registan** is the most famous square in Samarkand. It is surrounded on three sides by large **madrasas**. A madrasa is an Islamic college in which people used to learn religion, but also mathematics and astronomy. The buildings are decorated with tiles in many **shades of blue**, with patterns, lettering and stars. The old town is part of the UNESCO World Heritage.

Timur’s grandson **Ulugh Beg** ruled Samarkand in the 15th century. He was very interested in astronomy and had a large **observatory** built. In it stood a huge measuring instrument, part of which was sunk into the ground. With it the scholars measured the positions of over a thousand stars very precisely. A part of this instrument has survived to this day.

gewusst: Samarkand is about as old as Rome.
Ulugh Beg’s star catalogue was long regarded as one of the most accurate in the world.

teile.einleitung: The Leaning Tower of Pisa is one of the most famous towers in the world. It stands in the city of Pisa in Tuscany in Italy and leans clearly to one side. It is precisely this tilt that has made it world famous.
wichtigste: The tower stands in Pisa in Italy.
Building began in 1173 and took about 200 years.
The tower began to lean even during building.
It has eight storeys and is clad in white marble.
Today the top hangs about 4 metres to the side.
Visitors can climb to the top by a staircase of almost 300 steps.

abschnitte.text: The Leaning Tower is actually the **bell tower** of Pisa Cathedral. A free-standing bell tower is called a **campanile** in Italy. It stands together with the cathedral and the baptistery on a large square, the **Piazza dei Miracoli**, in English “Square of Miracles”. The tower has eight storeys, and the top one is the **belfry** with the bells. Since 1987 the square has been part of the **UNESCO World Heritage**.

Building began in **1173**. Again and again it was interrupted for long periods, for example because of wars. The tower was finished only about **200 years** later. The many pauses had an advantage: the soft ground could settle slowly and become firmer. The whole tower is clad in pale **marble** and therefore shines white in the sun.

The tower stands on soft ground of **clay and sand**. Already after the first storeys it sank on one side and began to **lean**. The builders tried to make up for this: they built the upper storeys slightly slanted. That is why the tower is even slightly curved. Today the top stands almost **4 metres** to the side of the foot.

In the 20th century the tower leaned more and more, and people feared it might topple over. That is why it was closed to visitors from **1990**. Experts carefully removed earth from under the higher side, so that the tower **straightened up** a little. Since 2001 it has been open again. Visitors climb up a **staircase** of almost 300 steps, and because of the tilt walking feels a little strange.

The famous scientist **Galileo Galilei** was born in Pisa in 1564. He studied how objects **fall**. A well-known story says he dropped balls from the Leaning Tower. Whether this was really so, however, is **not certain**. Even so, many people still link the tower with his falling experiments.

gewusst: Many tourists have themselves photographed as if they were holding the tower up with their hands.
The tower is not only leaning but also slightly curved, because the upper storeys were built slanted.
In Pisa there are other buildings that lean slightly because of the soft ground.

teile.einleitung: Snow is frozen water that falls from the sky in the form of flakes. In Switzerland it belongs to winter, especially in the mountains. Snow is lovely for playing and skiing, but as an avalanche it can also be dangerous.
wichtigste: Snowflakes consist of tiny ice crystals.
A typical snowflake has six arms.
Snow falls when it is cold enough in the clouds and on the ground.
On high mountains snow lies for a long time, because it is colder up there.
Glaciers form from snow that turns to ice.
An avalanche is snow that suddenly slides down a slope.

abschnitte.text: High up in **cold clouds** water vapour freezes into tiny **ice crystals**. The crystals grow in six directions. That is why a typical **snowflake** has six arms. If it stays cold on the way down too, the flakes fall to the ground as **snow** instead of rain. In great cold, light, dry **powder snow** forms, which blows up in a cloud when you ski.

The higher you climb, the **colder** it gets. That is why there is often snow on high mountains, even when it is already warm in the valley. If the snow lies for many years, it is pressed together and turns to **ice**. In this way a **glacier** forms, a great stream of ice that flows very slowly down the valley. Because the Earth is getting warmer, more ice melts than is newly added. That is why many glaciers, in Switzerland too, are getting smaller.

An **avalanche** is a large mass of snow that thunders quickly down a slope. It is very dangerous. In Switzerland the **Institute for Snow and Avalanche Research** in Davos watches the situation and issues the **avalanche bulletin**. Ski tourers carry an **avalanche transceiver**. It sends signals, so that rescuers can find buried people more quickly.

Children like to build a **snowman**. For this you roll three balls of snow and put them on top of one another. Often he gets a **carrot nose**. You can also go sledging, have a snowball fight or build an **igloo**. Snow sticks together best when it is a little damp.

A single ice crystal is actually **transparent**. In snow, however, countless crystals lie jumbled together. They throw the light back in all directions, which is why snow looks **white**. Fresh snow contains a lot of **air**. That is why it muffles sounds, and a blanket of snow protects plants on the ground from severe frost.

gewusst: No two snowflakes look exactly the same.
Because fresh snow swallows sounds, it is often especially quiet outside after a snowfall.

teile.einleitung: The Opera House in Sydney is one of the best-known buildings in the world. With its white roofs that look like sails, it is the landmark of Australia.
wichtigste: The Opera House stands on the harbour of Sydney in Australia.
The Danish architect Jørn Utzon won the competition in 1957.
Building began in 1959 and took about 14 years.
Queen Elizabeth II opened the Opera House in 1973.
The roofs are covered with more than a million ceramic tiles.
Since 2007 the Opera House has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

abschnitte.text: The roof is made up of several large, curved shells. Many people think of the **sails** of a ship, others of seashells. The shells are covered with small white and cream-coloured **ceramic tiles**. That is why they gleam in the sun and look slightly different depending on the light. The tiles are made so that the rain keeps them clean.

In 1957 the Dane **Jørn Utzon** won an international competition. His idea was bold, but nobody knew exactly how to build the curved roofs. Only after years was a solution found: the shells were put together from many identical parts. Because of arguments over costs and plans, Utzon left the project in 1966. Other architects finished the inside.

Building began in 1959 and was supposed to take only a few years. In the end it took about **14 years** and cost many times the planned amount. In **1973** Queen **Elizabeth II** opened the finished building. Today people agree that the great effort was worth it.

The Opera House stands on a **headland** in Sydney Harbour and is surrounded by water on three sides. Very close by, the **Sydney Harbour Bridge** spans the harbour. Because of its shape, people also call the steel arch bridge “the Coathanger”. Together, the Opera House and the bridge are one of the most famous photo subjects in Australia.

The Opera House has several halls for **opera, concerts, theatre and ballet**. Well over a thousand performances take place there every year. Many visitors also come just for a guided tour of the building. Since **2007** the Opera House has been a **UNESCO World Heritage Site**, just as, in Switzerland, the old town of Bern is, for example.

gewusst: Jørn Utzon never visited the finished Opera House himself.
More than a million tiles cover the roofs.

teile.einleitung: A shield volcano is a volcano with very flat, broad slopes. It looks like a shield lying on the ground. Shield volcanoes form from runny lava and mostly erupt rather calmly.
wichtigste: Shield volcanoes are flat and very broad.
They consist of runny basalt lava.
Their slopes are usually only 2 to 10 degrees steep.
Their eruptions are mostly calm, with lava flows and lava fountains.
The islands of Hawaii are huge shield volcanoes.
Olympus Mons on Mars is the largest known volcano in the solar system.

abschnitte.text: The name comes from the volcano **Skjaldbreiður** in Iceland. It means “broad shield”, because the mountain looks like a **warrior’s shield** lying on the ground. The whole type of volcano was named after it. Shield volcanoes are often much broader than they are high. Their slopes rise very gently, often only by **2 to 10 degrees**.

Shield volcanoes are built from **basalt lava**. Basalt is low in **silica** (SiO2); it contains only about 45 to 52 per cent of it. Little silica makes the magma **runny**. The lava therefore flows a long way before it solidifies. Layer upon layer, a broad, flat mountain forms. **Stratovolcanoes** such as Vesuvius are much steeper by comparison.

From runny lava the **gases** can escape easily. That is why large explosions are rare in shield volcanoes. The lava mostly flows out calmly in long **lava flows**, often with high **lava fountains**. This kind of eruption is called a **Hawaiian eruption**. When the surface of a lava flow solidifies, the molten rock beneath it flows on, well insulated. In this way **lava tubes** form, through which lava is carried many kilometres.

The best-known shield volcanoes on Earth stand on **Hawaii**. The islands are huge volcanoes that have grown upwards from the sea floor. They lie above a **hot spot** in the mantle. They include **Mauna Loa** and **Mauna Kea**. In **Iceland** too there are many shield volcanoes.

On Mars stands the largest known volcano in the whole solar system: **Olympus Mons**. It is a shield volcano and about **22 kilometres** high, measured from the mean level of the Martian surface. That is about two and a half times as high as **Mount Everest** above sea level. Because the surface on Mars does not shift, the lava could pour out at the same place for a very long time.

gewusst: Measured from the sea floor, Mauna Kea on Hawaii is higher than Mount Everest.
Through some old lava tubes you can walk on foot today.

teile.einleitung: The Richter scale is the best-known scale for stating the strength of earthquakes. It was developed in the USA in 1935 and is named after the seismologist Charles Richter.
wichtigste: The Richter scale is named after the seismologist Charles Richter.
Charles Richter and Beno Gutenberg presented it in 1935.
The value on the scale is called magnitude.
One step more means a deflection ten times greater on the seismogram.
The energy released is about 32 times as great per step.
The scale was originally calibrated for Southern California.
From about magnitude 6.5 the Richter scale becomes unreliable.

abschnitte.text: The American **seismologist** Charles Richter presented the scale in **1935** together with **Beno Gutenberg**. A seismologist is an expert on earthquakes. The two wanted to compare earthquakes in **Southern California** by their strength. For this they calibrated the scale for that region. Richter called the value the **local magnitude**.

A **seismometer** records the movements of the ground. The record is called a **seismogram**. The Richter magnitude refers to a particular instrument, the **Wood-Anderson seismometer**. The largest deflection is measured and converted to a distance of **100 km** from the **epicentre**. The epicentre is the point on the Earth’s surface directly above the focus of the earthquake.

The Richter scale is a **logarithmic scale**. This means: if the magnitude rises by one whole step, the deflection on the seismogram is **ten times** as great. An earthquake of magnitude 6 therefore has a deflection ten times greater than one of magnitude 5. The **energy** released is even about **32 times** as great. The scale has no fixed upper limit.

With very strong earthquakes the Richter scale reaches its limits. From about **magnitude 6.5** the measured values hardly rise any more, even though the earthquake is stronger. Experts call this **saturation**. That is why today the **moment magnitude** is usually used for large earthquakes. In the news, people still often talk about the Richter scale all the same.

In Switzerland too the ground shakes, but mostly so weakly that you do not feel it. The **Swiss Seismological Service** at ETH Zurich measures all the earthquakes in the country.
