About a quarter of the population does not have a Swiss passport, so many other languages are heard too.

Switzerland has long been **neutral** and takes no part in the wars of other countries. In Geneva many international organisations have their headquarters, such as the Red Cross, which was founded there in 1863, and a major seat of the UN. Switzerland is not in the EU, but has many treaties with it. Every year millions of tourists visit places such as the Matterhorn, the Jungfrau or Lucerne.

begriffe.erklaerung: One of the 26 member states of Switzerland, with its own government.
The seat of government and parliament; in Switzerland that is Bern.
The people themselves decide important questions in votes.
A state takes no side in the wars of other countries.

gewusst: Switzerland has no official capital; Bern is called the federal city.
On Swiss coins stands the Latin name “Helvetia” and not “Switzerland”.
Besides that of the Vatican, the Swiss flag is one of the two square national flags.

teile.einleitung: Gentle tourism is a way of travelling in which nature, landscape and local people are spared as far as possible. Visitors are meant to enjoy an area without harming it. In the Alps especially this is an important subject.
wichtigste: Gentle tourism means travel that spares nature and local people as far as possible.
Instead of by car, people often travel by train, bus, bicycle or on foot.
Local products, accommodation and offers are used.
The idea arose in the 1970s and 1980s.
In Switzerland there are several car-free holiday resorts.

abschnitte.text: In **gentle tourism** travellers are meant to get to know an area without burdening it. Nature is to stay protected, and local people are to benefit from tourism. The opposite is often called **hard tourism** or **mass tourism**: large hotel complexes, a lot of traffic and visitors who stay only briefly. The idea arose in the 1970s and 1980s, when many holiday resorts were being built up more and more.

Those who travel gently go on holiday, for example, by **train** or **bus** instead of by car or aeroplane. On the spot they get around on foot, by bicycle or by public transport. They stay in small hotels or on farms and eat **local products**. They keep to the paths, leave no rubbish behind and respect the customs of the people.

In Switzerland there are several **car-free holiday resorts**, for example **Zermatt**, **Saas-Fee**, **Wengen**, **Mürren** and **Braunwald**. They can be reached by train, cable car or PostBus. Many places offer guest cards with which you can use buses and trains cheaply. The Swiss tourism researcher **Jost Krippendorf** warned as early as the 1970s that too much building destroys the landscape.

Gentle tourism is often more expensive or more demanding than a package holiday. Some places, however, live precisely from many visitors. That is why communities look for a middle way between income and protection of nature. The visitors themselves, too, can achieve a great deal with their decisions.

gewusst: In Zermatt no ordinary cars run, only small electric vehicles.
The term “gentle travel” was made known around 1980 by the futurologist Robert Jungk.

teile.einleitung: A tourist attraction is a place or a building that is so special that people travel from far away to see it. It can be an ancient tomb, a giant statue, a city of rock or a modern building. Some attractions are so famous that almost every child recognises them in a photograph.
wichtigste: Attractions can be built by people or created by nature.
The Taj Mahal in India was built as a tomb.
The great statue of Christ on Mount Corcovado stands in Rio de Janeiro.
The rock city of Petra lies in Jordan.
France gave the USA the Statue of Liberty in New York.
The opera house with the sail-shaped roofs stands in Sydney harbour.
UNESCO includes especially valuable places in the World Heritage.

abschnitte.text: The **Taj Mahal** stands in the city of Agra in the north of India. The Mughal emperor Shah Jahan had it built in the 17th century as a **tomb** for his late wife Mumtaz Mahal. The building is of white marble and decorated with precious stones. Depending on the time of day it shimmers white, pink or golden. Every year millions of people visit this place.

The **statue of Christ** on Mount Corcovado looks out over the city of Rio de Janeiro in Brazil. It was completed in 1931 and is about 30 metres high, with its pedestal even about 38 metres. The **rock city of Petra** in Jordan was built about 2,000 years ago by the Nabataean people. Its temples and tombs were cut directly out of reddish sandstone. Famous above all is the Treasury, which you reach through a narrow gorge.

abschnitte.titel: Statue of Liberty and opera house
abschnitte.text: The **Statue of Liberty** stands on a small island off New York. France gave it to the USA, and it was inaugurated in 1886. The framework inside was designed by Gustave Eiffel, who later also built the Eiffel Tower in Paris. The **Sydney Opera House** in Australia was designed by the Danish architect Jørn Utzon and opened in 1973. Its white roofs recall sails in the wind.

**UNESCO** is an organisation of the United Nations for education, science and culture. It keeps a list of the **World Heritage** of humankind. On it are over 1,000 especially valuable places all over the world. The countries undertake to protect these places and to preserve them for later generations.

Switzerland too has many attractions. The World Heritage includes, for example, the **old town of Bern**, the Abbey of St Gallen, the castles of Bellinzona and the Rhaetian Railway over the Albula and the Bernina. World famous too are the **Matterhorn** near Zermatt, the Chapel Bridge in Lucerne and the Rhine Falls near Schaffhausen. Every year they attract many visitors from all over the world.

When very many people visit a place at the same time, it is called **mass tourism**. Then there are long queues, rubbish and sometimes damage to old buildings. That is why some places sell only a limited number of tickets. As a visitor you should not touch anything that is protected, and should not leave any rubbish behind.

begriffe.erklaerung: A building in which a dead person is buried and remembered.
An organisation of the UN that looks after education, science and culture.
Places that are so valuable to all humankind that they are given special protection.
Travelling in your free time to get to know other places.
A person who plans and designs buildings.

gewusst: The Statue of Liberty was originally copper brown; through wind and weather it turned green in time.
In Petra scenes of the film “Indiana Jones and the Last Crusade” were shot.
The statue of Christ in Rio is struck by lightning from time to time.

teile.einleitung: Dew is made of fine drops of water that form on grass, leaves and cars in the morning. It does not fall from the sky but forms directly on cold surfaces.
wichtigste: Dew forms directly on grass and other surfaces.
It forms when the air cools down during the night.
Water vapour from the air then condenses into drops.
Dew is a deposited form of precipitation.
If it is colder than zero degrees, frost forms instead of dew.

abschnitte.text: There is always invisible **water vapour** in the air. Cold air can hold less water vapour than warm air. On clear nights, grass, leaves and car roofs cool down strongly. When the air at these surfaces gets so cold that it can no longer hold the vapour, the vapour **condenses** into tiny drops. The temperature at which this happens is called the **dew point**.

abschnitte.titel: When there is a lot of dew
abschnitte.text: Most dew forms on **clear, windless nights**. Without clouds, the heat of the ground can radiate well into the sky. Clouds, on the other hand, act like a blanket and hold the warmth back. Wind mixes the air, so less dew forms when it is windy. In the morning the sun makes the drops **evaporate** again.

Rain, snow and hail fall from the sky. Dew, on the other hand, forms **right at the ground**. That is why it is called a **deposited form of precipitation**. If it is colder than zero degrees at night, fine ice crystals form instead of drops. This is **frost**, which covers meadows and trees in white.

Spiders' webs covered with dew glitter in the morning like strings of pearls. You can see the same process when a glass of cold water becomes wet on the outside. In very dry regions, dew is an important source of water for some plants and small animals.

gewusst: On meadows so much dew can form in one night that your shoes get completely wet as you walk.
Car windows are also often covered in dew in the morning, because they cool down quickly during the night.

teile.einleitung: An ice shelf is a huge plate of ice that floats on the sea but is still connected to the land. It forms from glaciers that flow from the land into the sea. Most ice shelves are found around Antarctica.
wichtigste: An ice shelf is a plate of ice that floats on the sea.
The ice comes from glaciers on the land.
Most ice shelves lie in Antarctica.
The largest is the Ross Ice Shelf, about as big as France.
The second largest is the Filchner-Ronne Ice Shelf.
The Larsen B ice shelf broke up within a few weeks in 2002.

abschnitte.titel: Ice that floats on the sea
abschnitte.text: In Antarctica huge **glaciers** flow slowly from the land into the sea. There they do not stop, but push out onto the water as a thick plate. This floating plate is called an **ice shelf**. It is usually **several hundred metres thick**. Because ice is lighter than water, it floats, but it stays frozen fast to the land.

Most ice shelves are found around **Antarctica**, with smaller areas in Greenland and the north of Canada too. The largest in the world is the **Ross Ice Shelf**. It is about as big as **France**. The second largest is the **Filchner-Ronne Ice Shelf** on the Weddell Sea. Together the ice shelves of Antarctica cover a huge area of sea.

abschnitte.titel: High walls of ice and icebergs
abschnitte.text: At the edge facing the open sea the ice shelf often forms a **high wall of ice** that rises steeply out of the water. Pieces keep breaking off there, which is called **calving**. In this way **tabular icebergs** form, which are flat like a table. Some of them are huge, even **bigger than the canton of Zurich**. They can drift for years through the Southern Ocean.

abschnitte.titel: When an ice shelf breaks up
abschnitte.text: In 2002 the **Larsen B** ice shelf on the Antarctic Peninsula broke up within a few weeks. It had already been getting thinner before that, because the air and the sea there were getting warmer. An ice shelf acts like a **brake** on the glaciers behind it. If it is missing, the glaciers flow faster into the sea, and the **sea level** rises. That is why researchers observe ice shelves closely with satellites.

gewusst: When floating ice shelf melts, the sea level hardly rises, much as a melting ice cube does not make a glass overflow.
Under some ice shelves fish and other animals live in complete darkness.

teile.einleitung: Roald Amundsen was a Norwegian polar explorer. In 1911 he was the first to reach the South Pole, and he is among the most famous explorers in history.
wichtigste: Amundsen first studied medicine, at his mother’s wish.
From 1903 to 1906 he was the first to sail through the whole of the Northwest Passage.
In 1910 he sailed with the ship Fram towards Antarctica.
On 14 December 1911 five men stood with him at the South Pole.
Dogs pulled the sledges of his expedition.
In 1926 he flew over the North Pole in the airship Norge.
In 1928 he lost his life on a rescue flight in the Arctic.

abschnitte.text: Roald Amundsen was born in 1872 in **Norway**. At his mother’s wish he began **studying medicine**. But even as a young man he dreamed of journeys into the eternal ice. After his mother’s death he gave up his studies and went to sea. He took part in an expedition to Antarctica and learned a great deal there about life in the cold.

The **Northwest Passage** is a sea route through the Arctic Ocean in the north of America. It connects the Atlantic with the Pacific. Many seafarers had tried in vain to sail through it. From **1903 to 1906** Amundsen was the first to succeed completely, with the small ship **Gjøa**. On the way he learned from the **Inuit** how to dress in the Arctic and how to travel with dogs.

In **1910** Amundsen sailed with the ship **Fram** towards **Antarctica**. At the same time the Briton Robert Falcon Scott was on his way to the South Pole. Amundsen relied on **sledge dogs** and on good skiers. On **14 December 1911** he reached the **South Pole** with four companions. So there were **five** of them, and they all returned safely.

abschnitte.titel: Over the North Pole by airship
abschnitte.text: Later Amundsen wanted to explore the Arctic from the air. In **1926** he flew over the **North Pole** in the **airship Norge**. On board with him were the Italian Umberto Nobile and the American Lincoln Ellsworth. In **1928** Nobile crashed in another airship in the Arctic. Amundsen flew off to help with the **rescue**, and never came back.

gewusst: The research station at the South Pole is called the Amundsen-Scott South Pole Station, after the two polar explorers.
The Fram, in which Amundsen sailed to Antarctica, stands today in a museum in Oslo.

teile.einleitung: With the Saffir-Simpson hurricane wind scale, hurricanes are divided into five categories according to their wind speed. In this way you quickly know how dangerous a storm is.
wichtigste: The Saffir-Simpson scale divides hurricanes into five categories.
What counts is the sustained wind speed.
Category 1 begins at about 119 km/h, category 5 at about 252 km/h.
From category 3 it is called a major hurricane.
The scale is named after Herbert Saffir and Robert Simpson.

abschnitte.text: The scale was developed in the USA in the early 1970s. It is named after the civil engineer **Herbert Saffir** and the meteorologist **Robert Simpson**. Simpson was then the head of the **National Hurricane Center** of the USA. A **hurricane** is a strong cyclone over the Atlantic or the eastern Pacific. In the western Pacific such storms are called **typhoons**.

The scale has **five categories**. What is decisive is the **sustained wind speed**. **Category 1** begins at about **119 km/h** and can, for example, break off branches and damage roofs. With each category the danger rises. **Category 5** begins at about **252 km/h** and can destroy houses completely. From **category 3** it is called a **major hurricane**.

abschnitte.titel: What the scale does not show
abschnitte.text: The scale measures only the **wind**. In a hurricane, however, **storm surges**, in which the sea pushes far inland, and heavy **rain** are also dangerous. That is why even a category 1 storm can cause great floods. Weather services therefore warn not only with the category, but also about water and rain.

gewusst: Hurricanes are given names, which according to fixed lists are given alternately to women and men.

teile.einleitung: The Sambadrome is a famous parade route in Rio de Janeiro. Here, at carnival, the great samba schools pass by with splendid costumes and floats. Tens of thousands of spectators sit in the stands.
wichtigste: The Sambadrome lies in Rio de Janeiro in Brazil.
It was opened in 1984.
The architect was Oscar Niemeyer.
The parade route is about 700 metres long.
At carnival the samba schools compete against one another here.

abschnitte.text: In the past the samba schools marched through ordinary streets of the city. Then in 1984 the **Sambadrome** was opened, a permanent parade route with stands on both sides. It was designed by the famous Brazilian architect **Oscar Niemeyer**. The route is about **700 metres** long. At the end lies a large square with a striking arch.

A **samba school** is not a school building but a club from a district of the city. All year round the members prepare their performance: music, dances, costumes and huge floats. At carnival each school passes through the Sambadrome for about an hour. A **jury** judges, for example, the music, costumes and floats. The best school becomes the winner of the carnival.

Outside carnival time concerts and other events also take place in the Sambadrome. At the **2016 Summer Olympic Games** in Rio the **archery** competitions were held here. In addition, the marathons started and finished there.

gewusst: A large samba school can march through the Sambadrome with several thousand dancers and musicians.
The parades often last the whole night until the morning.

teile.einleitung: The Selk'nam were an indigenous people who lived on the main island of Tierra del Fuego, right at the south of South America. They were hunters and lived mainly from hunting guanacos. They are also called the Ona.
wichtigste: The Selk'nam lived on the main island of Tierra del Fuego.
They are also called the Ona.
They hunted mainly guanacos, a kind of wild llama.
In the late 19th century they were almost wiped out through persecution and disease.
Today descendants of the Selk'nam live in Argentina and Chile.

abschnitte.titel: Life at the end of the world
abschnitte.text: **Tierra del Fuego** is a group of islands at the southern tip of South America. Today it belongs partly to **Argentina** and partly to **Chile**. On the large main island lived the **Selk'nam**, also called the **Ona**. The climate there is cool, windy and harsh. The Selk'nam moved through the land in groups and hunted mainly **guanacos** with bow and arrow. These are wild relatives of the llama. From their hides the Selk'nam made warm cloaks.

The Selk'nam had a rich culture with their own **stories** and **ceremonies**. At an important ceremony the men painted themselves with patterns and wore masks. In this way they represented spirits from their stories. The missionary and ethnologist **Martin Gusinde** visited the Selk'nam at the beginning of the 20th century and took photographs of this. These pictures are world famous today.

In the late 19th century many settlers came to Tierra del Fuego, also because of the **search for gold** and large **sheep farms**. The Selk'nam lost their land and were **persecuted**. In addition there were **diseases** that the immigrants brought in and against which the Selk'nam had no defences. Within a few decades they were almost wiped out. Today descendants are campaigning for their culture not to be forgotten.

gewusst: The photographs by Martin Gusinde of the painted Selk'nam are among the best-known pictures of Tierra del Fuego.

teile.einleitung: The Taj Mahal is a magnificent tomb of white marble in India. A ruler had it built for his late wife, and today it is regarded as one of the most beautiful buildings in the world.
wichtigste: The Taj Mahal stands in the city of Agra in India, on the River Yamuna.
The emperor Shah Jahan had it built as a tomb for his wife Mumtaz Mahal.
Shah Jahan was a ruler of the Mughal Empire.
The Taj Mahal is built of white marble.
Since 1983 it has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site, and since 2007 one of the New 7 Wonders of the World.

abschnitte.text: The Taj Mahal is a **tomb**, a building for someone who has died. The ruler **Shah Jahan** had it built for his wife **Mumtaz Mahal**, who died in 1631. He wanted to set up a monument to her that would remind people of her for ever. Later Shah Jahan himself was also buried in the Taj Mahal, **next to his wife**.

Shah Jahan was an emperor of the **Mughal Empire**. From the 16th to the 18th century this empire ruled large parts of India. The Mughal rulers had magnificent palaces, gardens and mosques built. Building the Taj Mahal took many years, and thousands of craftsmen worked on it.

The Taj Mahal is built of **white marble**. Fine patterns of coloured **gemstones** are set into the stone. Depending on the time of day, the building shimmers white, pink or golden. In front of the tomb lies a large garden with water pools in which the building is reflected. It stands in **Agra** on the bank of the **River Yamuna**.

Around the tomb stand **four** slender towers, the **minarets**. They lean slightly outwards. This way, if they ever collapsed, for example in an earthquake, they would **not fall onto the tomb**. So the builders planned very far ahead.

Since **1983** the Taj Mahal has been a **UNESCO World Heritage Site**. In **2007** it was chosen in a worldwide vote as one of the **New 7 Wonders of the World**. Millions of people visit it every year. Because the air in Agra is polluted, the marble has to be cleaned again and again.

gewusst: The name Taj Mahal is often interpreted as “Crown of the Palace”.
The grave of Shah Jahan is the only part of the interior that is not arranged symmetrically.

teile.einleitung: A seaport is a port on the sea in which large ships dock, are loaded and unloaded. A large part of world trade passes through seaports. The largest ports in the world today lie in Asia.
wichtigste: The largest container port in the world is Shanghai.
Singapore also has one of the largest container ports.
Jebel Ali in Dubai is the largest port in the Middle East.
Hamburg has the largest seaport in Germany.
Antwerp in Belgium has the second largest port in Europe.
The largest container port in the USA is Los Angeles.

abschnitte.text: In a seaport ships dock at **quays**, that is, at reinforced shores. Huge **cranes** lift containers from the ships onto lorries or railway wagons. This process is called **handling**. Many goods travel in standardised **containers**, large steel boxes in fixed sizes. They are counted in **twenty-foot equivalent units** (TEU). Besides containers, oil, grain, ore and cars are also handled.

The port of **Shanghai** in China has been the largest **container port** in the world since 2010. It handles well over 40 million standard containers a year. The city state of **Singapore** also has one of the largest container ports. It lies conveniently on one of the most important **shipping routes** between the Indian Ocean and the Pacific. In the Middle East **Jebel Ali** in Dubai is the largest port. It was built artificially.

The largest port in Europe is **Rotterdam** in the Netherlands. The second largest is in **Antwerp** in Belgium, on the Scheldt. Since the merger with Zeebrugge it has been called **Antwerp-Bruges**. The **Port of Hamburg** is the largest in Germany. It lies on the **Elbe**, about 100 kilometres from the North Sea. In Greece the Chinese state shipping company **COSCO** took over the majority of the port of **Piraeus** near Athens in 2016. For China, Piraeus is an important gateway to Europe.

The largest container port in the **USA** is **Los Angeles** (as of 2024). It lies on the Pacific coast right next to the port of **Long Beach**. A large part of the trade with **Asia** passes through these two ports. From there the goods are distributed across the country by train and lorry.

Switzerland has no seaport. Goods from overseas mostly arrive through the large ports on the North Sea, such as Rotterdam or Antwerp. From there many goods travel on **Rhine ships** as far as the **Rhine ports** in Basel. These ports are Switzerland’s gateway to the sea. Other goods come by train or lorry from ports in Italy or France.

gewusst: A large container ship can today load over 20,000 standard containers.
In modern ports some container vehicles drive entirely without a driver.

teile.einleitung: A maritime climate is the climate near the sea. Mild winters and cool summers are typical. The sea acts like a huge store of heat that evens out the temperatures.
wichtigste: A maritime climate prevails on coasts and on islands.
The winters are mild, the summers rather cool.
The sea stores heat and evens out the temperatures.
It often rains, and the sky is frequently cloudy.
Examples are Ireland and Brittany.
The opposite is the continental climate with hot summers and cold winters.

abschnitte.titel: The sea as a heat store
abschnitte.text: Water warms up more slowly than land and also cools down more slowly. In summer the **sea** takes in a lot of heat, and in winter it gives it off again. That is why the differences between summer and winter on the coast are **small**. Experts also call a maritime climate an **oceanic climate**. The air is damp, and it rains spread across the whole year.

A typical maritime climate is found in **Ireland**, in Great Britain, in **Brittany** in France and on the coast of Norway. In Ireland it is rarely very cold in winter, and snow hardly lies. In return it rarely gets really hot in summer. Because it rains a lot, the meadows there grow especially green. Ireland is therefore also called the “Emerald Isle”.

Far from the sea, in the middle of large continents, the evening-out influence of the water is missing. There the **continental climate** prevails. The summers are hot, the winters very cold, and it rains less. An example is the interior of Russia. The further you go from the sea, the more **continental** the climate becomes.

Switzerland lies between these two climates. With the **westerly winds** damp air often comes from the **Atlantic**, bringing rain and mild temperatures. From the east, by contrast, dry air that is very cold in winter can arrive. That is why in Central Europe people speak of a **transitional climate**. In Switzerland there are also the influences of the **Alps**, which shape the weather strongly.

gewusst: The Gulf Stream brings warm water to northern Europe, which is why many ports in Norway do not freeze over in winter.
On some coasts in Ireland and south-west England palm trees even grow outdoors.

tqlqd8x.t: Rhaetian Railway in the Albula/Bernina Landscapes

teile.einleitung: The Albula line and the Bernina line of the Rhaetian Railway lead through the mountains of the Grisons as far as Italy. Because of their daring structures and the beautiful landscape, they have been part of the UNESCO World Heritage since 2008.
wichtigste: The World Heritage route runs from Thusis to Tirano in Italy.
Switzerland shares this World Heritage site with Italy.
The Landwasser Viaduct near Filisur leads straight into a tunnel in the rock face.
At the Brusio spiral viaduct the train passes in a circle under itself.
The highest point of the Bernina line is at the Ospizio Bernina at 2,253 m above sea level.
The Rhaetian Railway runs on metre gauge.
The Bernina Railway manages a gradient of 70 per mille without a rack.

abschnitte.text: The **Rhaetian Railway** is the big railway company in the canton of the **Grisons**. Two of its lines were included in the **UNESCO World Heritage** in 2008 together with the surrounding landscape: the **Albula line** and the **Bernina line**. The route leads from **Thusis** via St. Moritz to **Tirano** in Italy. That is why Switzerland shares this World Heritage site with **Italy**. The lines were built at the beginning of the 20th century.

The Albula line connects Thusis with the Engadine. Its most famous structure is the **Landwasser Viaduct** near **Filisur**. The tall stone bridge leads in a curve straight into a **tunnel** in the rock face. At **Bergün** the train has to climb a great deal of height over a short distance. To do this it goes through **spiral tunnels** and loops in which it turns inside the mountain. After that it goes through the **Albula Tunnel** into the Engadine.

The Bernina line leads from St. Moritz over the **Bernina Pass** down to Tirano. Its highest point is at the **Ospizio Bernina** at **2,253 m above sea level**. On the way you see glaciers and mountain lakes. The railway manages gradients of up to **70 per mille**, and does so entirely without a rack. That means: over 1,000 metres of track it climbs 70 metres. This makes it one of the steepest railways of this kind.

In the Val Poschiavo stands the **Brusio spiral viaduct**. Here the train runs on a bridge in a **circle** and passes under its own track. In this way it gains height in a tight space without becoming too steep. The Rhaetian Railway runs on **metre gauge**: the rails lie one metre apart. That is narrower than on most railways and allows tighter curves in the mountains.

gewusst: The Glacier Express and the Bernina Express also run over the World Heritage route.
The Bernina line is regarded as the highest railway connection across the Alps.

teile.einleitung: The Rocky Mountains are the largest mountain range in the west of North America. They stretch over thousands of kilometres from Canada to the south of the USA and are the home of many wild animals.
wichtigste: The Rocky Mountains lie in North America.
They are often called “the Rockies” for short.
The name simply means “rocky mountains”.
The range runs from north to south.
Grizzly bears, pumas, beavers and bighorn sheep live there.
In Canada, Banff National Park lies in the Rocky Mountains.
The bald eagle, the national bird of the USA, also lives there.

abschnitte.text: The **Rocky Mountains** lie in the west of **North America**. They run from **north to south**, from Canada to the US state of New Mexico. The range is several thousand kilometres long. The name simply means **“rocky mountains”**. People often say **“the Rockies”** for short. The highest peak is Mount Elbert in Colorado, which is over 4,000 metres high.

An important **watershed** runs through the Rocky Mountains. This is a line at which it is decided where the rainwater flows. On one side the rivers flow into the **Pacific**. On the other side they flow into the **Atlantic** or into the Gulf of Mexico. Many great rivers rise in the Rockies, for example the Rio Grande.

Many large animals live in the Rocky Mountains. The **grizzly bear** is a mighty brown bear. The **puma** is a large wild cat that is very shy. The **bighorn sheep** has big, curved horns and climbs skilfully on steep rocks. In the streams the **beaver** builds dams of wood. In the sky the **bald eagle**, the national bird of the USA, circles.

In the Rocky Mountains there are many **national parks**. In Canada lie **Banff** and Jasper, with turquoise lakes and glaciers. Banff is the oldest national park in Canada. In the USA there is Rocky Mountain National Park in Colorado. The famous **Yellowstone National Park** with its hot springs also lies in the area of the Rockies.

gewusst: Yellowstone National Park in the Rockies is regarded as the oldest national park in the world.
With their dams, beavers can turn whole valleys into ponds.

teile.einleitung: A sand desert is a desert that consists mainly of sand and dunes. Many people imagine every desert like this. In fact most deserts are rather stony or rocky.
wichtigste: Sand deserts consist mainly of sand and dunes.
In Arabic a sand desert is called an erg.
By the geological classification, grains of sand are 0.063 to 2 millimetres in size.
The sand comes from weathered rock.
The wind carries and rolls the grains of sand and in this way forms the dunes.
The Erg Chebbi in Morocco has especially high dunes.

abschnitte.titel: Not every desert is made of sand
abschnitte.text: A desert is an area where it rains very little and hardly any plants grow. Many deserts, however, are **stony deserts** or **rocky deserts**. Even in the Sahara only about a fifth is covered with sand. Sand deserts are called by an Arabic word, **erg**. The largest continuous sand desert in the world is the **Rub al Khali** on the Arabian Peninsula.

Sand comes from **weathered rock**. In the desert it gets very hot by day and cold at night. As a result the stone expands and contracts again until it cracks. Wind, more rarely rain, and salt break it up further. By the geological classification, grains of sand are **0.063 to 2 millimetres** in size. Smaller grains are called silt, larger ones gravel.

The **wind** carries the grains of sand and makes them hop across the ground in small leaps. Larger grains it simply rolls along. Where the wind grows weaker, the sand stays put, and **dunes** grow. On the side facing the wind a dune is gentle, on the other side steep. In this way dunes can slowly migrate across the desert.

A well-known sandy area is the **Erg Chebbi** in Morocco, at the edge of the Sahara. Its dunes are up to over 100 metres high and glow orange and red in the evening. Many tourists ride into the dunes on dromedaries and spend the night in tents. Besides the sand there are small oases with date palms.

gewusst: Some dunes give off a deep humming when the sand slides down their slopes. They are called singing dunes.
The wind can carry Saharan sand as far as Switzerland, and then the sky turns yellowish.

teile.einleitung: Table Mountain is the famous local mountain of Cape Town in South Africa. Its flat summit looks like a giant table.
wichtigste: Table Mountain stands in Cape Town in South Africa.
It is a little over 1,000 metres high.
Its summit is as flat as a table.
The cloud above the summit is called the “tablecloth”.
A cable car takes you comfortably up the mountain.
The king protea, the national flower of South Africa, grows on the mountain.

abschnitte.text: Table Mountain rises straight up behind **Cape Town**. Its summit is an almost **flat plateau** several kilometres long, which is how it got its name. It consists mainly of hard **sandstone**. The highest point is **a little over 1,000 metres** above sea level. From the top you can see over the city and out to the **Atlantic Ocean**.

Often a thick white cloud lies over the summit and pours down over the edge. The people of Cape Town call it the “**tablecloth**”. It forms when damp sea air rises up the mountain and cools. Then the water vapour turns into cloud. When the tablecloth is there, visibility at the top is often poor.

If you do not want to hike, you take the **cable car** up. It has been running since 1929. The cabins of today turn once around themselves during the ride, so every passenger gets a good view. There are also many hiking trails that lead to the summit.

A special plant world grows on Table Mountain, the **fynbos**. Many of these plants are found only in the Cape region. They include the **king protea** with its large flower, the **national flower** of South Africa. **Rock hyraxes**, small animals with brown fur, bask in the sun on the rocks. They look like large guinea pigs, but are related to elephants.

gewusst: A constellation in the southern sky is named after Table Mountain: Mensa, the Table Mountain.
Since 2011 Table Mountain has been one of the “New 7 Wonders of Nature”.

teile.einleitung: The leap day is an extra day in the calendar, 29 February. It exists only in leap years, usually every four years. It makes sure that our calendar stays in step with the seasons.
wichtigste: The leap day is 29 February.
A year with a leap day is called a leap year, one without is called a common year.
Full centuries are leap years only if they are divisible by 400. That is why 1900 was not one.
In 45 BC Julius Caesar introduced a calendar with a leap day every four years.
Pope Gregory XIII had the calendar reformed in 1582.
In Switzerland, Zurich, Bern, Basel and Schaffhausen adopted the new calendar only in 1701.

abschnitte.text: The Earth needs about **365 days and almost 6 hours** for one trip around the sun. A normal calendar year, however, has only 365 days. Without a correction the calendar would fall a little further behind the sun every year. After a few centuries the **seasons would drift in the calendar**, and at some point Christmas would fall in summer. That is why every four years **29 February** is inserted.

In 45 BC **Julius Caesar** introduced the **Julian calendar**, with a leap day every four years. That was a little too much, however, because the year is somewhat shorter than 365 days and 6 hours. By the 16th century the calendar was therefore ten days out. **Pope Gregory XIII** had it reformed in 1582: 4 October was followed directly by 15 October, and the days from **5 to 14 October** were dropped.

In the **Gregorian calendar** a year is a leap year if it is divisible by 4. Full centuries such as 1700, 1800 or **1900**, however, are not leap years. The exception: if a century is divisible by 400, like 2000, it is a leap year after all. A year without a leap day is called a **common year**. Someone born on 29 February 2000 could celebrate a birthday on exactly that date **six times** up to the end of 2024: 2004, 2008, 2012, 2016, 2020 and 2024.

In Switzerland the Catholic places adopted the new calendar soon after 1582. The Reformed places **Zurich, Bern, Basel and Schaffhausen** followed only in **1701**. For a time neighbouring places therefore had different dates. Right at the end, the Grisons communities of **Schiers and Grüsch** changed in **1812**. They were thus the last in Western and Central Europe.

gewusst: Someone born on 29 February often celebrates on 28 February or on 1 March in common years.
The Gregorian calendar is not quite exact either: in about 3,000 years it will be out by about one day.

teile.einleitung: Sydney is the largest city in Australia. It lies on a large natural harbour bay on the east coast and is famous for its Opera House and the Harbour Bridge. The capital of Australia, however, is not Sydney but Canberra.
wichtigste: Sydney is the capital of the state of New South Wales.
The city lies on the natural harbour bay of Port Jackson.
The Opera House was designed by the Danish architect Jørn Utzon and opened in 1973.
The Harbour Bridge has the nickname “the Coathanger”.
In 1788 the first British convict colony was founded at Sydney Cove.
In 2000 the Summer Olympic Games took place in Sydney.

abschnitte.titel: A city on a natural harbour
abschnitte.text: Sydney lies on the east coast of Australia on the large bay of **Port Jackson**. It is regarded as one of the most beautiful **natural harbours** in the world. Sydney is the capital of the state of **New South Wales**. The capital of Australia as a whole is **Canberra**. More people live in Sydney than in any other Australian city.

The **Opera House** in Sydney is one of the best-known buildings in the world. The Danish architect **Jørn Utzon** won the competition for its design in **1957**. The roofs look like white **sails** or shells. The building work was difficult and took a long time. The Opera House opened in **1973**. Today it is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

The **Harbour Bridge** spans the harbour. It opened in **1932**. Because of its great steel arch, people in Sydney call it “The Coathanger”. Cars and trains cross the bridge, and pedestrians can walk over it. On New Year's Eve a huge firework display is set off here, which is shown on television all over the world.

Long before Europeans came, **Aboriginal people**, the first inhabitants of Australia, lived around the bay. In **1788** the “First Fleet”, a British fleet under **Arthur Phillip**, landed at **Sydney Cove**. The first British colony in Australia was founded there, mainly with **convicts** from Britain. For the Aboriginal people the colony brought great suffering, and they lost their land.

In **2000** the **Summer Olympic Games** took place in Sydney. They were the second Summer Games in Australia, because **Melbourne** had already hosted them in **1956**. The Games in Sydney are considered a great success. Many of the sports venues are still used today.

gewusst: Jørn Utzon never saw his finished Opera House himself, because he had left Australia before it was completed.
The Harbour Bridge is one of the largest steel arch bridges in the world.

teile.einleitung: Roraima is a huge table mountain in South America. It lies exactly where Venezuela, Brazil and Guyana meet, and with its steep walls it looks like an island above the clouds.
wichtigste: Roraima is a table mountain with a flat top and steep rock walls.
It lies at the meeting point of Venezuela, Brazil and Guyana.
Such table mountains are called tepui in the region.
Roraima is about 2,800 metres high.
It inspired the novel “The Lost World” by Arthur Conan Doyle.

abschnitte.text: Roraima is a **table mountain**. That means: its summit is flat like a tabletop, and almost vertical **rock walls** fall away at the sides. Such mountains are called **tepui** in the region. Roraima is about 2,800 metres high. It lies at the **meeting point of three countries**, **Venezuela**, **Brazil** and **Guyana**. It is made of very old sandstone.

abschnitte.titel: A world of its own up above
abschnitte.text: On the summit it rains very often, and clouds often hang over the mountain. Many **waterfalls** plunge down the rock walls. Up there is hardly any soil, but mainly bare rock with strange shapes. Because the summit is so cut off, special **plants** grow there that exist only on such table mountains. They include meat-eating plants.

Roraima inspired the British writer **Arthur Conan Doyle** to write an adventure novel. In **“The Lost World”** explorers travel to a remote table mountain in South America. There, in the book, dinosaurs still live. That is of course made up. Today hikers climb Roraima in several days.

gewusst: The word “tepui” comes from the language of the Pemón, a people who live in this region.

teile.einleitung: The Zambezi is the fourth longest river in Africa. It flows through the south of the continent into the Indian Ocean. On it lie Victoria Falls and two of the largest reservoirs in Africa.
wichtigste: The Zambezi is the fourth longest river in Africa, after the Nile, the Congo and the Niger.
It rises in Zambia and flows into the Indian Ocean in Mozambique.
It flows through or along six countries.
For long stretches it forms the border between Zambia and Zimbabwe.
Lake Kariba and the Cahora Bassa reservoir supply a lot of electricity.
Victoria Falls are among the largest waterfalls in the world.

abschnitte.titel: A long way to the sea
abschnitte.text: The Zambezi is about 2,600 kilometres long and so the **fourth longest river in Africa**. It rises in the north-west of **Zambia**. After that it flows through or along **six countries**: Zambia, Angola, Namibia, Botswana, Zimbabwe and Mozambique. Over a long stretch it forms the **border between Zambia and Zimbabwe**. In Mozambique it flows into the **Indian Ocean** with a broad delta.

On the border between Zambia and Zimbabwe the Zambezi plunges over **Victoria Falls** into a narrow gorge. The falls are over 1.5 kilometres wide. The spray rises so high that you can see it from far away. The local people call the falls Mosi-oa-Tunya, which means “the smoke that thunders”. Further upriver the **Kazungula Bridge** has connected Botswana and Zambia since 2021.

Two mighty dams were built on the Zambezi. **Lake Kariba** between Zambia and Zimbabwe was created at the end of the 1950s and, by volume of water, is one of the largest reservoirs in the world. Further downstream the **Cahora Bassa** dam in Mozambique holds back the river. Both power stations produce a lot of **electricity** for the region.

In the Zambezi and on its banks live **hippos**, **crocodiles** and many fish. **Mana Pools** National Park in Zimbabwe is part of the UNESCO World Heritage. In the dry season many **elephants**, buffalo and antelopes come to the water there. Many tourists explore the river by canoe.

In the west of Zambia the Zambezi floods a wide plain every year. Then the king of the **Lozi** people leaves his palace and travels in a large boat to higher ground. This solemn journey is called the **Kuomboka**. Many rowers, drums and spectators accompany the king.

gewusst: Victoria Falls are about twice as high as Niagara Falls.
Lake Kariba is so big that in many places you cannot see the other shore.

teile.einleitung: Many people work in a different country from the one in which they grew up. Often they send part of their wages to their families back home. This money is called remittances.
wichtigste: Remittances are money that migrants send to relatives in their country of origin.
In German they are called “Rücküberweisungen”.
In 2024, according to the World Bank, about 685 billion US dollars flowed into low and middle income countries.
India received the most remittances in 2024.
In Tajikistan their share of the economy was highest in 2024.
They exceed direct investment and development aid put together.
The UN wants to bring the fees down to below 3 per cent by 2030.

abschnitte.text: A **remittance** is money that **migrants** send to their relatives in their **country of origin**. Families often need the money for food, rent, school or visits to the doctor. From **Switzerland**, too, many people regularly send money to their countries of origin. Often these are small amounts, but they are very important for the recipients.

Taken together, the many small transfers add up to enormous sums. According to the **World Bank**, in **2024** about **685 billion US dollars** flowed into low and middle income countries. That is more than the **direct investment** by firms and **development aid** put together. In 2024 **India** received the most money. In relation to the size of the economy, the share was highest in **Tajikistan**.

In the **Philippines** very many people work abroad, for example on ships, in hospitals or in households. They are called **Overseas Filipino Workers**, that is, Filipino workers overseas. The money they send is very important for the country’s economy. With it many families can give their children a better education.

Money can be sent through banks, special **transfer services** or, today, often by mobile phone. **Fees** are charged on this. According to the **UN Sustainable Development Goals**, these costs are to fall to **below 3 per cent** by **2030**. There is also an old, informal system called **hawala**. It is based on **trust** between money brokers, who credit amounts to one another.

Remittances help many families directly and can reduce poverty. But experts also name possible **downsides**. A country can become **dependent** on money from abroad. In addition, the **pressure on the government** to improve its own economy may fall. Moreover, the country often lacks exactly the young, well-educated workers.

gewusst: With the hawala system money can change hands without the money itself travelling across the border.
For some countries remittances are one of the most important sources of income of all.

teile.einleitung: Robinson Crusoe Island is a small island in the Pacific that belongs to Chile. It is named after a famous character from a novel, whose story is based on a real sailor.
wichtigste: Robinson Crusoe Island belongs to Chile.
It lies in the Pacific, far off the Chilean coast.
It belongs to the Juan Fernández archipelago.
The sailor Alexander Selkirk lived here alone for several years.
His story inspired the novel “Robinson Crusoe” by Daniel Defoe.

abschnitte.text: Robinson Crusoe Island lies in the **Pacific Ocean**, several hundred kilometres off the coast of **Chile**. It belongs to the **Juan Fernández archipelago**, a small group of islands. The island is mountainous and has steep coasts. There is only one small village, called San Juan Bautista. The island used to be called Más a Tierra, and later it received its present name.

At the beginning of the 18th century the Scottish sailor **Alexander Selkirk** was left behind on the island. He had quarrelled with his captain. Selkirk lived there **alone for several years**, until a ship picked him up. His story became known in England. The writer **Daniel Defoe** then wrote the novel **“Robinson Crusoe”**, which appeared in 1719.

On the Juan Fernández Islands many **plants** grow that exist only here. Some animals too live only on these islands, for example a special **hummingbird**. That is why the nature there is under **protection**. A neighbouring island is today called **Alejandro Selkirk Island**, after the real sailor.

gewusst: In the book the character Robinson Crusoe lives on his island much longer than Selkirk did in reality.

teile.einleitung: Salvador is a large port city in the north-east of Brazil and the capital of the state of Bahia. It was the first capital of Brazil. Its old town and its Afro-Brazilian culture are world famous.
wichtigste: Salvador was founded by the Portuguese in 1549.
From 1549 to 1763 Salvador was the capital of Brazil.
The city lies on the large bay Baía de Todos os Santos.
The old town Pelourinho is part of the UNESCO World Heritage.
Many residents have African ancestors.
The lift Elevador Lacerda connects the upper town and the lower town.

abschnitte.text: In 1549 the **Portuguese** founded Salvador on the bay **Baía de Todos os Santos**, which means All Saints’ Bay. The city became the first **capital** of the colony of Brazil. Sugar, tobacco and later gold were shipped out through the port. In 1763 the Portuguese moved the capital to **Rio de Janeiro**, which was closer to the gold mines.

The old town **Pelourinho** lies on a hill above the sea. It has colourful houses from colonial times, narrow cobbled lanes and many magnificent churches. Since 1985 it has been part of the **UNESCO World Heritage**. The upper town and the lower town by the port are separated by a steep slope. The **Elevador Lacerda**, a large lift, takes people up and down in a few seconds.

During colonial times very many people from Africa were taken to Salvador as **slaves**. That is why many residents today have African ancestors. Their culture shapes the city to this day: music with drums, the martial art **capoeira** and the religion **Candomblé**. A popular dish is **acarajé**, deep-fried bean fritters.

The **carnival** of Salvador is one of the largest street festivals in the world. Unlike in Rio, huge lorries with loudspeakers and bands move through the streets here. Behind them thousands of people dance. The festival lasts several days and attracts visitors from all over Brazil and from abroad.

gewusst: Salvador is often called the African heart of Brazil.
The Elevador Lacerda overcomes a difference in height of about 70 metres.
